Designing Machine Learning Systems (Chip Huyen, O'Reilly, 2022). The book-length version of this note's framework: data, features, deployment, monitoring and continual learning. Read the chapters on deployment and data distribution shifts first.
Rules of Machine Learning (Martin Zinkevich, Google). Short numbered rules for building a first pipeline, choosing objectives and handling skew. Good for quotable judgement calls; an hour's read.

Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (Sculley et al., NeurIPS 2015). Why the model is a small box in a large system: entanglement, feedback loops, glue code, configuration debt. The vocabulary interviewers borrow when they ask about maintenance.

The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso, Communications of the ACM, 2013). Where the fan-out arithmetic of section 02 comes from, and hedged and tied requests as fixes. Read before any question on latency.

Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations (Covington, Adams and Sargin, RecSys 2016). The two-stage candidate generation and ranking design, with practical choices about labels and freshness. The classic citation for section 04.

Practical Lessons from Predicting Clicks on Ads at Facebook (He et al., ADKDD 2014). Click prediction at scale: boosted trees feeding logistic regression, data freshness, online learning and negative downsampling. Read with the ads design in section 05.

System Design for Recommendations and Search (Eugene Yan, 2021). How several companies split offline and online work and retrieval and ranking, compared side by side. A quick tour of real architectures.
Point-in-time joins (Feast documentation). How an open-source feature store implements the join of section 03, including TTLs and filtering out late-written values.

Answer out loud first, then open the answer. Each answer stands on its own: the short answer, the mechanism, the trade-off, the likely follow-up. Questions 6, 10, 11, 15, 16, 17, 19 and 22 are hand drills; do them with a pen. Questions 12 and 25 to 27 are the “what if” follow-ups that come after a design.
The question and the framework
1How do you approach an ML system design question?
Clarify, then go from the goal to metrics, data, features, model, serving, evaluation and monitoring, with numbers at each step.
Clarify: the decision the prediction drives, the output, the scale, the latency budget at p99, how fresh things must be, cost and constraints (privacy, regulation). State assumptions as numbers.
Metrics: business goal → an online metric an experiment can move, plus guardrails → an offline metric that tracks it at the operating point.
Formulation, data and labels: what exactly is predicted; where labels come from, how late, and how the current system biased them.
Features by entity and freshness tier; a baseline before the model; serving with a latency budget and sizing; evaluation out of time, then shadow, then A/B; monitoring and retraining.
Close with trade-offs and what version two would add.
Follow-up: “why not start with the model?” Because the model depends on the latency, the label and the number of items, which come first. (01)
2Which clarifying questions do you ask first, and why each?
Only those whose answers change the design: about four to six, then assume the rest out loud.
Is someone waiting? Decides online or batch, and the latency budget.
How many items? Thousands can be scored directly; millions need a retrieval stage.
How fast does the world change? New items an hour or adversaries mean streaming features and frequent retraining.
Where do labels come from, and how late? Decides proxies, training windows and monitoring before labels.
What does each mistake cost? Sets thresholds and whether calibration matters.
Is there a system today? It's the baseline, and shadow mode is the migration path.
Follow-up: privacy, regulation and explainability limit features and model class; ask when the domain suggests them (lending, health, payments). (01)
3How do you go from a business goal to an offline metric? Use a feed.
A chain: a slow business goal, an online metric a two-week test can move, and an offline metric chosen because it tracks the online one.
Business: long-term retention and satisfaction.
Online: sessions per user per day, quality-weighted time spent, meaningful interactions; guardrails on hides and reports, creator exposure, latency.
Offline: per-head AUC, log loss and calibration of the engagement predictions, nDCG@20 on logged sessions.
Why these: the value formula adds the heads' probabilities, so they must be calibrated; nDCG weights the top positions users actually see.
The check: across past launches, did offline gains predict online ones? If not, fix the offline metric before trusting it.
Follow-up: logged sessions favour the ranker that made them, so offline metrics filter candidates and the A/B test decides. (01, 05)
4You have 45 minutes. How do you spend them, and what is being scored?
Every step covered, reaching serving by about minute 25, then depth where the interviewer pulls; scored on navigation, ML depth, systems depth, trade-offs, operations and communication.
A plan: 5 minutes clarifying, 5 on metrics, 5 on formulation and labels, 5 on features, 5 on baseline and model, 8 on serving, 5 on evaluation, 4 on monitoring, 3 on summary and next steps.
Hand over the steering: offer two areas to go deeper on and let the interviewer choose.
Park explicitly: “cold start matters; I'll come back to it.”
Red flags: starting with the architecture of the model; no numbers; no baseline; stopping at deploy; 30 minutes on one step.
Follow-up: at senior levels, expect to be judged on prioritization: what you'd build first and what you'd defer. (01, 01)
5Batch, online or streaming inference: when each? Give a hybrid.
Batch when the decision can wait, online when someone is waiting and the request matters, streaming when results must follow events within minutes without blocking a request.
Batch: a scheduled job writes predictions to a store; cheap and easy to audit, but up to a day stale and blind to new users. Nightly churn scores, recommendation emails.
Online: the model runs in the request on fresh features; costs latency and availability. Search, feed ranking, payment authorization.
Streaming: runs per event, asynchronously, writing results for later requests. Flagging an account after a burst of logins.
Hybrid feed: item embeddings and the ANN index precomputed, user long-term embeddings nightly, session features streamed, ranking online.
Numbers: batch-scoring 100M monthly users × 500 candidates is 5 times 10^10 a day; online is 500M requests × 500 = 2.5 times 10^11 , five times more, but fresh and aware of context.
6Hand drill: size the feed. 50M daily users, 10 loads each, 3× peak, 200 ms, 500 candidates at 2 MFLOP, 10M items and 100M users with 128-dim embeddings.
About 17,400 requests a second at peak, 3,500 in flight, 350 busy cores for the ranker, 5 GB of item embeddings, 51 GB of user embeddings.
Requests: 50M times 10 = 500M a day; ÷ 86,400 = 5,787 a second on average; × 3 = 17,361 at peak.
In flight (Little's law): 17,361 × 0.2 s ≈ 3,472.
Ranker: 500 × 2 MFLOP = 1 GFLOP a request; at an assumed 50 GFLOP/s per core that's 20 ms of one core; 17.4 TFLOP/s at peak ≈ 347 cores busy, about 700 at 50% utilization.
Memory: items 10M × 128 × 4 B = 5.12 GB (fits on one machine, so replicate the index); users 100M × 128 × 4 B = 51.2 GB (a sharded store).
Logs: 500M × 20 impressions × 500 B = 5 TB a day.
Follow-up: “and with 10× traffic?” See question 27. (02)
7p99 latency is over budget. Where do you look, and what do you change?
Trace per-stage p99s, then attack fan-out, feature fetches, candidate count and queueing, in roughly that order.

Fan-out: with N parallel calls, 1 - 0.99^N of requests hit some call's slowest 1%: 9.6% at 10 calls, 63% at 100. Batch per-candidate calls into one multi-key fetch per shard; hedge slow calls after their p95 (at most about 5% extra load); accept partial results.
The ranker: fewer candidates, a light ranker in front, distillation or quantization, compute the user side once per request.
Queueing: latency climbs steeply near full utilization; keep headroom, autoscale, shed load at peak.
Caching helps the mean, not the tail: 80% hits at 1 ms and misses at 40 ms give a mean of 8.8 ms but a p99 of about 40 ms (the miss path's p95).
Follow-up: “percentiles of stages don't add”: summing sequential p99s overstates, while fan-out makes the max worse. (02, 02)
8What should happen when the model or a feature service times out?
A fallback decided in advance, never a silent default, and the fallback rate monitored like a metric.
Timeouts per dependency, below the stage budget; circuit breakers stop calling a failing service for a while.
A feed's ladder: rank what arrived → the user's last good feed from cache → popular in the region.
Payments: rules alone; approve small amounts, step up or refer large ones. Failing closed blocks good customers; failing open is what attackers wait for.
Train for it: if features can be missing at serving, the model must have seen missing values in training.
Follow-up: in an A/B test, a heavier model times out more and its arm partly serves the fallback; compare fallback rates per arm before reading the result. (02)
9What is a feature store? Why two stores? When don't you need one?
A registry of feature definitions feeding an offline store (full history, for training) and an online store (latest values, for serving).
Two stores because the access patterns are opposite: training scans history across all keys; serving looks up one key in milliseconds.
Materialization pushes the latest batch values online; the stream processor writes both.
What it buys: one definition for both paths (less skew), point-in-time training sets, features shared with owners, freshness monitoring.

Not needed for a single batch model with a few features: a tested pipeline is enough. It pays off with several online models sharing features, or streaming features that must match between training and serving.

10Hand drill: rows F1, F2, F3 are written at 02:00 on 3, 4 and 5 Jan, each covering data to the previous midnight (values 12·0, 14·0, 31·1). The job then fails until 9 Jan. Join payments at 03 Jan 15:00, 04 Jan 01:30, 04 Jan 21:00 and 08 Jan 12:00, with a 48-hour TTL.
F1, F1, F2, missing. Join on when each row became available, and drop values older than the TTL.
T2, 04 Jan 01:30: F1, not F2. F2's data ends at midnight, but it wasn't written until 02:00; serving at 01:30 still held F1. Joining on data time gives training a value serving never had.
T4, 08 Jan 12:00: the newest row, F3 (the job failed after it), covers data to 5 Jan 00:00, 84 hours earlier: past the TTL, so missing, as the online store would return.
The naive latest-row join gives 31·1 to every payment, including the dispute the fraud itself caused: label leakage.
Follow-up: late-arriving records also leak, so filter on when each record was written, not only on its event time. (03)
11How do you compute “payments on this card in the last hour” in real time? How much memory for 100 million cards?
A stream processor keeps per-card bucketed windows (or decayed counters) keyed by card, updated per event by event time, and writes them to the online store.

Bucketed sliding window: 60 one-minute buckets, each a count and a sum (4 B each): 480 B per card; error at most one bucket (1/60 of the window). 100M cards: 48 GB for this window; with a 24-hour window of hourly buckets as well (192 B), 67.2 GB.

Decayed counter: c leftarrow c\,e^-Delta t/tau + 1 , 16 B per feature; events at minutes 0, 10, 20 read at 30 with tau = 60 : 0.607 + 0.717 + 0.846 = 2.17. Three such features: 4.8 GB. Soft edge instead of a hard window.
Event time and watermarks: aggregate by when payments happened; a watermark (say 2 minutes) decides what's too late.
Parity: decide whether the current payment counts, and do the same in training (replay the log through the same code, or log the served values).
12What if a feature goes stale: the streaming job lags two hours?
Detect it from freshness, not from the model; serve “missing” past the TTL to a model that learned what missing means; tighten the policy while blind; then backfill.
What breaks: velocity counters freeze or read 0, and 0 looks innocent, so a fraud model gets more lenient exactly when it's blind. A feed loses session signals and gets generic.
Detect: the age of the newest value per feature, the stream consumer's lag, jumps in zero or null rates, a shift in the score distribution.

Handle: past the TTL the store returns missing; the model was trained with missing values, so it leans on other features. For critical features, switch to a fallback model trained without them, or tighten rules (more step-ups) until it recovers.
Recover: replay the event log so the online store catches up, and mark that period in the training data (or exclude it) so training doesn't see fresh values where serving saw stale ones.
Follow-up: alert before the TTL, with an owner and a runbook. (03)
13Why separate retrieval and ranking? Show the arithmetic.
The precise model can afford a few hundred candidates per request, not millions, so a cheap high-recall stage must cut the catalogue first.
Heavy ranker on 10M items: 10M × 2 MFLOP = 20 TFLOP a request, 400 core-seconds; about 7 million cores at 17,400 requests a second.
Exact dot products over 10M 128-dim embeddings: 2.56 GFLOP and 5.1 GB read per request: already more than ranking 500 candidates.
ANN (about 10,000 vectors) → light ranker on 1,500 → heavy ranker on 500: about 1.03 GFLOP a request, about 360 busy cores.
Different jobs: retrieval optimizes recall@K, ranking orders the top with cross features, re-ranking shapes the page.
Follow-up: retrieval recall caps the system: if it's 60%, the ranker never sees 40% of the good items. Measure each stage. (04)
14How does a two-tower retrieval model work, how is it trained, and what can't it do?
Two networks embed users and items separately; the score is their dot product, so item vectors can be precomputed and searched with ANN.
Serving: item vectors computed offline and indexed; the user vector computed per request (or cached); ANN returns the top few hundred.
Training: (user, engaged item) pairs, softmax over in-batch negatives; popular items appear as negatives more often, so subtract the log of each item's sampling probability (logQ correction).
Negatives: random catalogue items (easy), in-batch (free, popularity-biased), hard negatives (sharper, but include false negatives).
Limit: the towers meet only at the dot product, so no user × item cross features. That's why it retrieves and a ranker orders.
Follow-up: new items are retrievable on day one if the item tower uses content features (text and image embeddings), not just IDs. (04, 04)
15Hand drill: item A shown at position 1 (examination 1.0) gets 100 clicks in 1,000 impressions; item B at position 3 (examination 0.4) gets 60 in 1,000. Which is more relevant?
B: 15% against A's 10%, once each click is weighted by the inverse of its position's examination probability.
Model: P(click) = theta_position times r_item .
Naive click rates: A 10%, B 6%, so a model on raw clicks ranks A first and keeps generating evidence for A.
Estimating theta : swap items between positions for a small random slice of traffic and compare the same items' click rates.
Alternative: position as a training feature, fixed to 1 at serving.
Follow-up: exposure bias: unseen items have no labels, and “not clicked” only counts as negative if it was likely seen. (04)
16Hand drill: the true click rate is 1% and you kept 10% of non-clicks for training. What does the model predict on average, and how do you fix it?
About 9.2%; correct it by adding the log of the kept share to the predicted log-odds.
Correction: logit p = logit p_s + log q : -2.293 + ln 0.1 = -2.293 - 2.303 = -4.595 , so p = 1.0\% .
Why it matters: the order is unchanged, so AUC doesn't notice, but auction prices, value formulas and cost thresholds use the number itself.
Why downsample at all: at billions of impressions, the non-clicks are mostly redundant; keeping 10% cuts training cost almost tenfold for little loss.
Follow-up: change the sampling rate and forget the correction, and every score shifts overnight with no change in ranking metrics. (04)
17How do you add diversity and business rules without wrecking relevance? Work MMR on four posts.
A re-ranking stage after the ranker: hard filters, soft constraints, exploration slots, and a greedy diversity rule such as MMR.
MMR: lambda\,rel(i) - (1 - lambda)max_j in Ssim(i, j) , picking greedily.
Rules: filters (seen, blocked, policy), spacing (no more than two from one creator in a row), fixed ad slots, a fresh post in the top ten.
Tuning lambda is an A/B question: diversity often costs a little short-term engagement and buys retention.
18Design real-time payment fraud detection.
Online scoring inside the authorization: rules plus a boosted-tree model on request, streaming and batch features, three actions from costs, labels from chargebacks.
Scale: 20M payments a day, 231 a second average, about 1,160 at peak; 50 ms at p99; fraud about 0.05%, 1 in 2,000.
Metrics: total cost (fraud loss plus friction); online fraud basis points, decline and step-up rates; offline value-weighted recall at a fixed false-positive rate, PR-AUC, calibration.
Labels: chargebacks and reports over weeks to months; train on matured windows; step-up outcomes label the grey zone.
Features: velocity windows per card, device and IP; the card's spending profile; merchant risk; shared-device graph features.
Model and rules: rules for policy and speed against new attacks; boosted trees for the grey area; keep all frauds and 2% of good payments, then correct the probabilities.
Serving: one batched feature read (10 ms), rules, a 5 ms model; on timeout, rules decide, with small amounts approved and large ones stepped up.
Monitoring: decline and step-up rates by merchant hourly, feature freshness, early reports; rules daily, retraining weekly to monthly.

19Hand drill: approving costs pA ; stepping up costs ₹20 of friction for a good customer and lets 10% of fraud through; declining a good customer costs ₹200. Where are the cut-offs for ₹500, ₹5,000 and ₹50,000?
Approve below c_s / ((1 - ell)A + c_s) , decline above (c_d - c_s)/(ell A + c_d - c_s) , step up between.
Costs: approve pA ; step up (1 - p)20 + 0.1\,pA ; decline (1 - p)200 .
₹500: approve below 20/470 = 4.26%; decline above 180/230 = 78.3%.
₹5,000: approve below 20/4,520 = 0.44%; decline above 180/680 = 26.5%.
With only approve and decline: decline above 200/(200 + A): 28.6%, 3.85%, 0.40%.
Needs calibrated probabilities, after undoing any downsampling.
Follow-up: why not decline everything flagged? At 60% recall and 0.2% false positives that's 6,000 frauds against 39,980 good payments a day, 13% precision. (05)
20Design a feed ranking system.
A funnel: multi-source retrieval, a light ranker, a multi-task heavy ranker, re-ranking; trained on debiased impression logs, evaluated by A/B with a long-term holdout.
Scale: 50M daily users, 17,400 requests a second at peak, 10M posts, 200 ms at p99, 20 posts a load.
Metrics: retention; sessions and quality time online; hides, reports and creator exposure as guardrails; per-head AUC, log loss and nDCG offline.
Pipeline: follows, two-tower ANN, co-engagement, trending and fresh → about 1,500 → light ranker 500 → heavy ranker 50 → re-rank 20.
Ranker: heads for click, dwell, like, share, hide, combined by product-chosen weights; cross features; position handled in training.
Freshness: streaming engagement counts, hourly index rebuilds with inserts for new posts, daily retraining.
Risks: feedback loops and popularity bias (exploration, diversity), interference through shared creators in tests.
21How do you handle cold start for new users and new items?
Content and context features instead of IDs, plus a bounded budget of exploration.
New users: onboarding choices, popular items for their language and region, device and context; streaming session features let the feed adapt within the first session.
New items: content embeddings (text, image) make them retrievable and rankable before any engagement; ID embeddings learn later.
Exploration: reserve a small share of impressions for new items, allocated bandit-style, so each gets enough impressions for its engagement rate to be estimated, then earns or loses exposure.
Avoid the trap of a ranker that only trusts items with history: the loop starves new creators.
22Hand drill: ad A bids ₹20 with true CTR 1%; ad B bids ₹10 with CTR 2.5%. Run the second-price auction with calibrated predictions, then with A's CTR predicted twice too high.
Calibrated: B wins and earns ₹200 per 1,000 impressions. With A over-predicted, A wins and earns only ₹125.
eCPM: 1000 times b times widehatCTR : A 200, B 250.
Calibrated: B wins, pays 20 times 0.01 / 0.025 = 8 , ₹8 per click; 25 clicks per 1,000 impressions, ₹200.
A at 2%: A's eCPM 400 wins; pays 10 times 0.025 / 0.02 = 12.5 , ₹12.50 per click; its real CTR is 1%, so 10 clicks and ₹125 per 1,000. Revenue falls 37.5% and users get a worse ad.
Every ad 2× too high: winner and price unchanged (the ratio cancels), but reserve prices, blending with organic content, budget pacing and conversion bids all use the absolute number.
So: check the calibration ratio (predicted ÷ actual clicks) per ad, advertiser and segment, and log loss next to AUC.
23Design an LLM-powered customer-support assistant.
Route, retrieve, generate grounded answers, act through authorized tools, guard input and output, and hand off with a summary; measure resolution, satisfaction and repeat contacts.
Scale and latency: 50,000 conversations a day, six turns; first token within about 1.5 s for chat.

Path: mask personal data and screen injections → intent routing (sensitive cases to people) → hybrid retrieval and reranking over the knowledge base, with query rewriting → a grounded, cited answer → tools (order status, refunds within limits) with authorization in the tool service → output policy checks → handoff on low confidence, repeated failure, user request or sensitive intent.
Metrics: containment and task success, CSAT, repeat contact within 7 days, escalation; guardrails on wrong refunds and invented policies.
Cost (assumed prices): about $0.013 a turn, $0.077 a conversation, $3,825 a day; $2,610 with prefix caching; small next to human contacts avoided.
Failure modes: stale knowledge base, retrieval misses papered over, injection, tool abuse, abandonment counted as resolution, personal data in logs.
24How do you evaluate the support assistant before and after launch?

Offline: a golden set from real conversations, scored by a judge validated against humans, with retrieval and generation scored separately. Online: an A/B test on resolution, satisfaction and repeat contacts, plus sampled judging and human review.
Golden set: real resolved conversations by intent, plus hard, adversarial and out-of-scope cases; the expected answer or action for each.
Judging: a rubric (correct, grounded in the cited passage, policy-compliant, right action, right handoff) scored by an LLM judge whose agreement with human labels has been measured.
Stages separately: retrieval recall@k, then answer faithfulness given the retrieved passages, then tool-call accuracy, so a failure points to its stage.
Gate every change (prompt, model, knowledge base) on the regression suite.

Online: randomize by user; read containment together with CSAT and 7-day repeat contacts, since containment alone rewards users giving up; judge a sample of live transcripts; send low scores to human review.
Follow-up: failures from escalations feed new golden cases and knowledge-base fixes. (05)
25What if the latency budget halves?
Measure where the time goes, then precompute more, score fewer candidates with a cheaper model, and cut fan-out; accept a measured quality loss.
Trace per-stage p99s first; cut the biggest stages, not all evenly.
Precompute: cache user embeddings and candidate lists; bundle a user's features under one key so it's one fetch.
Rank less: 500 → 250 candidates halves the heavy ranker (20 ms → 10 ms of one core); strengthen the light ranker (distilled from the heavy one) so the cut loses little.
Cheaper model: quantize or distill; GPU batching.
Tails: one multi-get per shard, hedged requests, partial results from slow sources.
Price it: measure the offline loss of each cut (nDCG with 250 vs 500 candidates) and confirm with an A/B test.
26What if labels arrive 30 days late?
Train on matured windows, validate with a matching gap, monitor through proxies and drift, and keep the fast parts of the system (features, rules) fresh.
Training: the newest usable labels are 30 days old; never count recent unlabelled events as negatives (label delay).
Validation: an out-of-time split with a 30-day gap shows the decay you'll actually face.
Proxies: early signals (customer reports, failed verification, early engagement), checked on old data to rank models the same way as the final label.
Monitoring without labels: data quality, feature and score drift, proxy metrics.
Stay current anyway: streaming features carry today's behaviour into a month-old model; rules react to new attacks within minutes.
Experiments take at least 30 days longer to read on the true metric; pre-register a validated proxy.
Modelling: treat unlabelled recent events as censored (a time-to-event or delayed-feedback model) instead of dropping them.
27What if traffic grows tenfold?
Redo the sizing, scale the stateless parts out, re-shard the stateful ones, and lower the cost per request.
Sizing: 174,000 requests a second at peak; the ranker needs about 3,500 busy cores (about 7,000 at 50%) unless the cost per request falls.
Ask which tenfold: ten times the users means ten times the keys (feature store and embedding memory grow too); ten times the requests per user means the same keys, more reads.
Stateless: rankers and retrieval replicas scale horizontally; the 5 GB item index is replicated, not sharded.
Stateful: more online-store shards and replicas; more stream partitions; logs at 50 TB a day, so sample what's logged.
Cost per request: caching gets more effective with more traffic; fewer candidates; cheaper models; larger GPU batches.
Tails: more shards means more fan-out; batch fetches, hedge, autoscale and shed load.
28Online learning or periodic retraining? And how do you roll back a bad model?
Periodic retraining by default, online updates where items and labels move in minutes; rollback is a registry switch that takes the features and the policy with the model.
Periodic: simple, reproducible, easy to gate and audit; stale between retrains. Suits slow labels (credit, most fraud).

Online: fresh within minutes; suits ads, news, trending content. Risks drift from bad data or attacks, feedback amplification, and hard reproduction; needs a streaming label join, continuous evaluation and frequent snapshots.
Middle ground: periodic full retrains plus frequent updates to embeddings of new IDs, bias terms or a calibration layer.
Rollback: keep the previous model warm and switch by config. Roll back the calibrator and thresholds with it, keep the old feature definitions served, and remember decisions already made stay made.
Before it's needed: canary with automatic rollback on guardrails.

Clarify (decision, output, scale, p99 latency, freshness, cost, constraints) → business goal → online metric + guardrails → offline metric that tracks it → formulation and labels (definition, delay, bias) → features by tier → baseline → model → serving (mode, budget, sizing, fallbacks) → offline, shadow, A/B → monitoring, retraining, feedback loops → version two. Serving by about minute 25, then depth.

beginaligned QPS_peak &approx k cdot fracDAU times requests per user86,400, quad k approx 2–3 \\ in flight &= QPS times mean latency \\ compute &= QPS times candidates times FLOP per candidate \\ memory &= N times d times bytes endaligned
Feed: 17,400 QPS peak; 3,500 in flight; 1 GFLOP a request, about 350 busy cores; items 5.1 GB, users 51 GB, features 160 GB raw; logs 5 TB a day.
beginaligned P(some call in its slowest 1\%) &= 1 - 0.99^N \\ mean with cache &= h\, t_hit + (1 - h)\, t_miss endaligned

N = 10, 50, 100: 9.6%, 39.5%, 63.4%. Cache 80% at 1 ms and 40 ms: mean 8.8 ms, p99 still about 40 ms. Batch fetches, hedge after p95 (about 5% extra load), partial results, headroom. Every dependency: timeout + fallback; monitor the fallback rate.
beginaligned feature(k, t) &= latest row with t_available le t, if t - t_data le TTL \\ c_new &= c_old\, e^-(t - t_last)/tau + 1 endaligned

Tiers: batch (hours), streaming (seconds–minutes), request-time. Offline store = history for training; online store = latest values for serving. Bucketed window: 60 × 8 B = 480 B per key. Same staleness and TTL in training as in serving; a stale counter reads 0, so prefer missing.

beginaligned value(i) &= sum_k w_k\, P(action_k) - w_hide\, P(hide) \\ MMR(i) &= lambda\,rel(i) - (1 - lambda)max_j in Ssim(i, j) \\ P(click mid i, k) &= theta_k\, r_i, quad hat r_i = tfrac1n_itextstylesum 1/theta_k \\ logit p &= logit p_s + log q endaligned

10M → ~1,500 (recall) → 500 → 50 (order) → 20 (the page). Heavy ranker on everything: 20 TFLOP a request; the funnel: about 1 GFLOP. Two-tower: no cross features. Negatives: random, in-batch (logQ), hard (false negatives). 1% CTR with 10% of negatives kept → 9.17%.
beginaligned p_1 &= fracc_s(1 - ell)A + c_s, quad p_2 = fracc_d - c_sell A + c_d - c_s \\ eCPM &= 1000 cdot b cdot widehatCTR \\ price per click_1 &= b_2\, widehatCTR_2 / widehatCTR_1 endaligned

Fraud ₹5,000: approve below 0.44%, step up to 26.5%, decline above. Ads: A over-predicted 2× → revenue ₹200 → ₹125 per 1,000. Support bot: $0.0765 a conversation at assumed prices; the risk is quality, so measure containment with CSAT and repeat contacts.

Checks at ingestion, features and serving. Pseudonymize, minimize, delete everywhere. Fairness: action and error rates by group; calibration within groups, equal precision and equal error rates conflict when base rates differ. Cost next to lift. Registry: model + data + feature versions + calibrator + thresholds; canary; rollback by config. Periodic retraining by default, online updates for fast items.

How it differs from a p-value

chunks.x: Hypothesis testing, A/B tests and power · Deepam Minda

A p-value is the chance of data at least this extreme if there were no effect. It is not the chance that there's no effect, and it says nothing about size. A test and a confidence interval are the same calculation: the 95% interval holds every effect the test wouldn't reject at 5%.

Power is the chance of catching an effect that is really there. For a two-sided 5% test with 80% power you need about 16sigma^2/delta^2 users per arm, so halving the smallest effect you care about quadruples the sample. Small tests that “win” overstate the effect, sometimes several times over.

Pick the test by the question and the unit, not by habit. Welch's t for means, the two-proportion z (the same as a 2×2 chi-square) for rates, Fisher or exact binomial for small counts. Mann–Whitney tests whether one group tends to be larger, not whether its mean is. Permutation tests and the bootstrap cover what has no formula.

The central limit theorem makes the average normal, not the data, and skew slows it down: a rough rule is n ge 25gamma^2 . Whale-driven revenue needs capping, variance reduction or a lot of users; a log or a trimmed mean answers a different question.

An A/B test is mostly plumbing: a salted hash for assignment, analysis at the unit you randomized (or the delta method), a sample-ratio check, full weeks, and CUPED, which shrinks variance by a factor 1 - rho^2 . Marketplaces and social products break the independence the maths assumes.

Every extra look and every extra metric is another lottery ticket. Checking daily for two weeks turns 5% false positives into 22%. Use a fixed horizon or alpha spending, Holm or Benjamini–Hochberg for many metrics, and know that a Bayesian “probability B is better” doesn't make peeking free. Without randomization, every method rests on an assumption the data can't fully check.

A hypothesis test is proof by contradiction, with noise. Assume nothing happened, work out what results chance alone would produce under that assumption, and ask whether what you saw looks like one of them. If it would be very unusual, you drop the assumption.

The running example. A checkout change is tested on 20,000 users split evenly. Control: 1,000 of 10,000 convert (10.0%). Treatment: 1,080 of 10,000 convert (10.8%). Did the change work, or is a 0.8-point gap the kind of thing that happens by chance?

The null hypothesis H_0 : the “nothing happened” claim, stated precisely enough to compute with: p_B = p_A . The alternative H_1 is what you'd believe instead: p_B ne p_A (two-sided) or p_B gt p_A (one-sided).
A test statistic: one number measuring how far the data sit from H_0 , in units of noise.

Its sampling distribution under H_0 : how that number would spread across many repeats of the experiment if H_0 were true. For differences in averages the central limit theorem makes it close to a standard normal.
The p-value: where the observed statistic falls in that distribution.
The significance level alpha and a decision rule fixed before looking: reject H_0 when p le alpha .

For the running example, the statistic is the gap divided by its standard error (SE), the typical size of the gap's wobble from sample to sample. Under H_0 both groups share one rate, so it's estimated from both groups together (“pooled”):

beginaligned hat p &= fracx_A + x_Bn_A + n_B = frac208020000 = 0.104 \\ SE_0 &= sqrthat p\,(1 - hat p)Big(frac1n_A + frac1n_BBig) = 0.00432 \\ z &= frachat p_B - hat p_ASE_0 = frac0.0080.00432 = 1.85 endaligned

In words: if the change did nothing, both groups would convert at about 10.4%, and a gap between two groups of 10,000 would typically wobble by 0.43 points. The observed gap of 0.8 points is 1.85 wobbles from zero.
The p-value is the probability, computed assuming H_0 is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. Here “extreme” means lvert z rvert ge 1.85 in either direction:
beginaligned p &= Pbig(lvert Z rvert ge 1.85 mid H_0big) \\ &= 2\,big(1 - Phi(1.85)big) = 0.064 endaligned

In words: Phi is the standard normal's cumulative probability. If the change truly did nothing, about 6.4% of experiments like this one would show a gap of 0.8 points or more, in one direction or the other.
What it is not. Each of these is a common wrong reading:

Not the probability that H_0 is true. The p-value is computed assuming H_0 ; it can't also be its probability. That probability depends on how many tested ideas actually work. If 10% of ideas work and tests have 80% power, then among results with p lt 0.05 , 36% are false positives (0.9 × 0.05 = 0.045 false against 0.1 × 0.8 = 0.08 real). With 30% power it's 60%.
Not “the probability the result is due to chance”. That's the same mistake in other words.

Not an effect size. A trivial 0.05-point lift (0.5% relative) with ten million users per arm gives z = 3.7 and p = 0.0002 ; a large lift on 200 users may not reach significance. Report the estimate and its interval, not just p.
1 - p is not the probability the effect is real, or that it will replicate.

p gt 0.05 is not evidence of no effect. Here the interval below runs up to +1.65 points, a 16% relative lift. Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, unless the test had the power to see the effect you care about.

Under H_0 , p-values are uniform. Every value between 0 and 1 is equally likely, so 5% of experiments with no effect land below 0.05 and 1% below 0.01. That's what alpha means, and it's why an A/A test (section 06) should produce a flat histogram of p-values.

“p = 0.064, so there's a 6.4% chance the change does nothing.” No: it's a 6.4% chance of a gap this big if the change does nothing. Turning that around needs a prior on how often changes work, which is the Bayesian calculation in section 08.

alpha is chosen before the data: the false-positive rate you accept when H_0 is true. Rejecting when p le 0.05 is the same as rejecting when lvert z rvert ge 1.96 , since 5% of a standard normal lies beyond ±1.96. Here 1.85 falls short, so the result is not significant at 5%.

0.05 is a convention, not a law. Set alpha by what each mistake costs. An irreversible, expensive launch deserves a stricter alpha . A guardrail that protects against harm (crash rate, refunds) often uses a looser one, because missing harm is the costlier error there. The critical values worth knowing:
A one-sided test puts all of alpha in one tail, so the bar drops from 1.96 to 1.645. For the running example the one-sided p-value is 0.032, which would be “significant”.

When one-sided is legitimate: it's decided before the data, and a result in the other direction would lead to the same action as no result. “Ship only if it's better” fits; so does a non-inferiority check (“the new model is not worse than the old by more than 0.2 points”). You give up the right to claim harm.

Why switching after seeing the data is p-hacking: if you pick the tail that matches the observed direction, you'll “find” an effect whenever lvert z rvert gt 1.645 in either direction. That happens 10% of the time under H_0 , so the real alpha is 0.10 while you report 0.05.
The default is two-sided, because a change can hurt, and you want to know when it does.

chunks.h: Tests and confidence intervals are one calculation
chunks.x: A 95% confidence interval is the set of effect sizes that a 5% test would not reject. So “the interval excludes 0” and “ p lt 0.05 for H_0\!: delta = 0 ” are the same statement. For the gap, using each group's own variance (no H_0 to assume):

chunks.h: Tests and confidence intervals are one calculation
chunks.x: beginaligned SE &= sqrtfrachat p_A(1 - hat p_A)n_A + frachat p_B(1 - hat p_B)n_B = 0.00432 \\ CI_95 &= 0.008 pm 1.96 times 0.00432 \\ &= [-0.0005,\ 0.0165] endaligned

chunks.h: Tests and confidence intervals are one calculation
chunks.x: In words: the data fit anything from a 0.05-point loss to a 1.65-point gain. The interval contains 0, matching p = 0.064 . It also shows what the p-value hides: the result is uncertain, not “no effect”.

chunks.h: Tests and confidence intervals are one calculation
chunks.x: What the “95%” means. It describes the procedure: over many repeats of the experiment, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true effect. A given interval either contains it or doesn't. It is not “a 95% probability that the true lift is between −0.05 and +1.65 points”; that is the reading of a Bayesian credible interval (section 08), which with a flat prior and large samples happens to give nearly the same numbers.

chunks.h: Tests and confidence intervals are one calculation
chunks.x: The small mismatch: the test used the pooled SE (computed as if H_0 were true) and the interval the unpooled one. Here both round to 0.00432; when the rates differ a lot they differ slightly, and a borderline result can disagree. Duality is exact when the same SE is used.

chunks.h: Tests and confidence intervals are one calculation
chunks.x: One-sided tests pair with one-sided bounds: the one-sided 5% test matches the lower bound 0.008 - 1.645 times 0.00432 = 0.0009 , which is above 0.

chunks.h: Tests and confidence intervals are one calculation
chunks.x: The same test in another form: a chi-square test on the 2×2 table (converted or not, by group) gives chi^2 = 3.43 = 1.85^2 and the same p = 0.064 . With one degree of freedom, chi-square is z squared.

A non-significant result doesn't show that two versions are the same. To claim that, turn the hypotheses around so that “different” is the null, using a margin m : the largest difference you'd treat as no difference.
Non-inferiority: H_0 : the new version is worse by at least m . Reject (conclude “not worse”) when the one-sided 95% lower bound of the difference is above -m .

Equivalence, by two one-sided tests (TOST): test H_0\!: delta le -m and H_0\!: delta ge m , each one-sided at 5%. Claim equivalence if both reject, which is the same as the 90% interval lying inside (-m, m) .

Example. A cheaper model converts 0.1 points worse than the current one, SE 0.15 points, margin 0.5 points. The usual test gives p = 0.51 , “no significant difference”, which on its own proves nothing. The 90% interval is -0.1 pm 1.645 times 0.15 = [-0.35, +0.15] , inside ±0.5, so both one-sided tests reject ( p = 0.004 and 0.00003 ): equivalent within the margin, and so also non-inferior. With an SE of 0.5 points the usual test would still say “not significant”, but the interval [-0.92, +0.72] would establish nothing.

Say it in an interview: “I'd report the lift with its 95% interval, here +0.8 points with an interval from −0.05 to +1.65. The p-value of 0.064 says a gap this big would turn up about 6% of the time with no real effect, so it's not significant at 5%, but the interval shows the test can't rule out a lift worth having. It's underpowered rather than negative.”
Truth: real effect ( H_1 )
Test says: effect (reject H_0 )
Type I error, false positive. Rate alpha
Correct. Rate 1 - beta , the power
Type II error, false negative. Rate beta
Effect size can be absolute (+0.8 points), relative (+8%) or standardized: the gap divided by the standard deviation (Cohen's d = delta/sigma ).

The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is the smallest true effect the test is designed to catch with the chosen power. It's a business choice, the smallest lift worth shipping, made before the test, not read off the result.

Power is the probability of rejecting H_0 when the true effect is some specific size. It isn't one number: it's high for big effects and near alpha for tiny ones. When people say “80% power”, they mean at the MDE.

Mixing up significance and power. alpha is about worlds with no effect: how often you'd cry wolf. Power is about worlds with an effect of a given size: how often you'd notice it. A test can have alpha = 5\% and 20% power at the same time, and most underpowered tests do.

The test statistic's distribution in two worlds. Grey: no effect. Blue: the true lift equals the MDE. The critical line (dashed) is set by alpha alone, and beta is the part of the blue bell that falls short of it. Making both errors small at once means pulling the bells apart: more users, less variance, or a bigger effect.

Read the picture as a tug of war. Moving the line right (smaller alpha ) shrinks the orange tails but grows beta . The only way to shrink both is to move the blue bell further right, and its centre sits at delta/SE : the true effect measured in standard errors.

Setup: two arms of n users each, a metric with per-user variance sigma^2 in both arms, and a true difference delta between the arms' means. Each arm's mean has variance sigma^2/n , and the variances of independent things add when you subtract them, so the gap has SE = sqrt2sigma^2/n .
Under H_0 , z = gap/SE is standard normal, and the test rejects when z gt z_1-alpha/2 (1.96), or below -1.96 .
Under H_1 , the gap's mean is delta instead of 0, so z is normal with mean delta/SE and standard deviation 1. That's the blue bell.
Power is the share of the blue bell beyond 1.96. The far tail below −1.96 is negligible for any useful power, so power = Pbig(Z gt z_1-alpha/2 - delta/SEbig) = Phibig(delta/SE - z_1-alpha/2big) .
Set power to 1 - beta . Phi(x) = 1 - beta exactly when x = z_1-beta (0.84 for 80%), so the centres must be z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta standard errors apart: 1.96 + 0.84 = 2.80.
Substitute the SE and solve for n .

beginaligned fracdeltasqrt2sigma^2/n &= z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta \\ n &= frac(z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta)^2 cdot 2sigma^2delta^2 \\ &= frac(1.96 + 0.84)^2 cdot 2sigma^2delta^2 approx frac15.7\,sigma^2delta^2 approx frac16\,sigma^2delta^2 endaligned

In words: users per arm grow with the noise sigma^2 and shrink with the square of the effect. The 16 is just 2 times 2.80^2 rounded up: the factor 2 is there because there are two noisy means, and 2.80 is the distance the bells must be apart.
Worked numbers. Baseline conversion 10%, so sigma^2 = p(1 - p) = 0.09 ; alpha = 0.05 two-sided, power 80%:

Halving the lift from 0.5 to 0.25 points quadruples the users, because n propto 1/delta^2 . The last column uses the pooled rate under H_0 and each arm's own p(1-p) under H_1 , as most calculators do; planning with the baseline variance is within about 3.5% of it.

The running example's power. With 10,000 per arm, SE = sqrt2 times 0.09 / 10000 = 0.00424 . If the true lift were 0.8 points, delta/SE = 1.89 and power is Phi(1.89 - 1.96) approx 0.47 . Even if the change truly works as well as it looked, the test had less than an even chance of saying so. Turned around, the MDE for a given n is delta = 2.80sqrt2sigma^2/n : 1.19 points at 10,000 per arm, 0.53 at 50,000, 0.38 at 100,000.

Days, not just users. Divide the total users by the daily traffic entering the test and round up to whole weeks: 44,150 users at 20,000 a day is 2.2 days, but the test should still run a full week so every weekday is represented (section 06).
Starting from the design above (22,075 per arm, 80% power for a 0.8-point lift), changing one thing at a time:
True effect is half the MDE
Variance halved (CUPED with rho approx 0.71 )
alpha = 0.01 instead of 0.05
the line moves out to 2.58
the line moves in to 1.645
z_1-beta goes from 0.84 to 1.28
90/10 split instead of 50/50 (same total)
SE propto sqrt1/f + 1/(1-f) , smallest at f = 0.5
Variance reduction is the cheapest lever: it buys the same power as more users without waiting longer. Section 06 shows how.

chunks.h: Why underpowered tests mislead: the winner's curse
chunks.x: With 10,000 per arm, a result can only be significant if the observed lift exceeds 1.96 times 0.00424 = 0.83 points. Suppose the true lift is a modest 0.25 points. Most runs fall short; the few that clear the bar are the ones where noise pushed the estimate far up. Conditioning on significance selects the lucky draws:

chunks.h: Why underpowered tests mislead: the winner's curse
chunks.x: Significant results overstate it by (Type M)

chunks.h: Why underpowered tests mislead: the winner's curse
chunks.x: Significant results with the wrong sign (Type S)

chunks.h: Why underpowered tests mislead: the winner's curse
chunks.x: In words: a Type M (magnitude) error is the exaggeration ratio, the average size of a significant estimate divided by the true effect. A Type S (sign) error is a significant result pointing the wrong way. At low power, “significant” mostly means “lucky”, so the reported lift is inflated and later shrinks: the launch delivers less than the test promised.

chunks.h: Why underpowered tests mislead: the winner's curse
chunks.x: Fixes: power the test for a realistic effect, not a hoped-for one; distrust big lifts from small tests; shrink estimates towards what past experiments typically found (a Bayesian prior, section 08); replicate surprising wins.

chunks.h: Why underpowered tests mislead: the winner's curse
chunks.x: “Post-hoc power” doesn't help. Power computed from the observed effect is a fixed function of the p-value (a p of 0.05 always gives about 50%), so it adds no information. Power is a design quantity, computed for the MDE before the test.

Every test in this section has the same skeleton: an estimate, its standard error, their ratio, and a reference distribution. What changes is the data type, how the standard error is computed, and which reference distribution is honest for the sample size. The decision table at the end of the section collects them.
For a mean with unknown spread, the statistic divides by the sample standard deviation s :
t = fracbar x - mu_0s / sqrt n
In words: how many estimated standard errors the sample mean is from the hypothesised value mu_0 .

Why not just use 1.96: s is itself an estimate, and at small n it's noisy. When it comes out too small, t gets too big, so t has heavier tails than a normal. If the data are normal, t follows Student's t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom, which accounts for exactly that extra noise.

How much it matters: the 5% two-sided critical value is 2.571 at 5 degrees of freedom, 2.228 at 10, 2.042 at 30, 1.984 at 100 and 1.962 at 1,000. Using 1.96 on a one-sample test with n = 5 gives a 12% false-positive rate instead of 5%; at n = 10 , 8%; at n = 30 , 6%.
At A/B-test sizes they coincide. With thousands of users per arm, t and z are the same number, which is why online experiments talk about “z-tests” for means too.
The fine print: t is exact only for normal data. For small, skewed samples neither t nor z is exact, and a permutation or exact test (below) is safer.

A one-sample t-test compares one mean with a fixed value (is average delivery time above the 30-minute promise?). A paired t-test is a one-sample t-test on within-unit differences: the same users before and after, the same queries scored by two models, twins.
Why pairing is so powerful. Eight users' weekly sessions, before and after a change:
Paired: the differences average 1.2 with standard deviation 0.48, so SE = 0.48/sqrt 8 = 0.17 , t = 7.0 , p = 0.0002 .
Treated as two unrelated groups (Welch): SE = 1.81 , t = 0.66 , p = 0.52 .

Same data, opposite conclusions. Users differ from each other by a lot (standard deviation about 3.5) while the change moves each of them by about 1.2. The unpaired test has to see the change through all that between-user spread; pairing subtracts each user's own baseline and removes it:
Var(after - before) = sigma_a^2 + sigma_b^2 - 2rho\,sigma_a sigma_b

In words: when before and after are strongly correlated ( rho = 0.99 here), subtracting cancels almost all the variance. CUPED (section 06) is the same trick for A/B tests, where each user is only in one arm but their pre-experiment behaviour plays the role of “before”.
The non-parametric version is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which ranks the absolute differences and compares the rank sums of positive and negative ones.

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: Both compare two means with t = (bar x_1 - bar x_2)/SE . They differ in the SE:

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: beginaligned Student:quad s_p^2 &= frac(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2n_1 + n_2 - 2 \\ SE_Student &= s_p sqrtfrac1n_1 + frac1n_2 \\ SE_Welch &= sqrtfracs_1^2n_1 + fracs_2^2n_2 endaligned

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: In words: Student assumes both groups share one variance and estimates it by pooling, weighted by sample size. Welch lets each group keep its own variance, and adjusts the degrees of freedom (the Welch–Satterthwaite formula) for the extra uncertainty:

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: nu_Welch = fracbig(s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2big)^2dfrac(s_1^2/n_1)^2n_1 - 1 + dfrac(s_2^2/n_2)^2n_2 - 1

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: In words: the degrees of freedom land between the smaller group's n - 1 and n_1 + n_2 - 2 , and near the low end when a small group is the noisy one, because then the SE leans on a few noisy points. For the example below (10 users at sd 3, 40 at sd 1) it's 9.5.

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: What breaks when the variances differ. Group 1 has 10 users with standard deviation 3; group 2 has 40 users with standard deviation 1. Pooling weights by size, so the pooled variance (2.5) is dominated by the big, quiet group, and Student's SE comes out at 0.56 when the honest one is 0.96. Simulated with no true difference:

chunks.x: Big group is the noisy one (40 at sd 3, 10 at sd 1)

chunks.x: Equal sizes, unequal spread (25 at sd 3, 25 at sd 1)

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: Why Welch is the default: when Student's assumption fails, it is either wildly anti-conservative (26% false positives) or wastefully conservative (0.1%, so it loses power). When the assumption holds, Welch loses almost nothing: with 20 per group and a true half-standard-deviation difference, power was 33.9% for Welch against 34.0% for Student. Testing for equal variances first and then choosing is worse than always using Welch, because the pre-test has its own errors.

chunks.h: Two independent groups: Student vs Welch
chunks.x: With equal group sizes Student is fairly robust, which is why the problem hides in balanced A/B tests and bites in unbalanced ones (a 90/10 rollout with a noisier treatment).

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: Two-proportion z-test: the running example. Use the pooled SE for the test (it's computed under H_0 , where the rates are equal) and the unpooled SE for the interval. It needs a handful of successes and failures in each arm (a common rule: at least 10 of each).

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: Chi-square test of independence: are two categorical variables related? Compare observed counts O in each cell of a table with the counts E expected if they were independent (row total × column total / grand total). For a 2×2 table it's the two-proportion z-test squared.

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: Chi-square goodness of fit: do counts match a fixed expected split? The sample-ratio-mismatch check (section 06) and “is this die fair?” are this test.

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: chi^2 = sum_cells frac(O - E)^2E

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: In words: each cell's surprise, squared and scaled by how big that cell was expected to be. Degrees of freedom: (r-1)(c-1) for an r times c table, and categories − 1 for goodness of fit. Example: 600 rolls of a die giving 90, 110, 95, 105, 120 and 80 against 100 each: chi^2 = (100 + 100 + 25 + 25 + 400 + 400)/100 = 10.5 on 5 degrees of freedom, p = 0.062 . Not enough to call the die loaded.

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: Small counts: Fisher's exact test. The chi-square approximation needs expected counts of about 5 or more per cell. Fisher's test fixes the table's margins and computes the exact probability of each possible table (a hypergeometric distribution), so it needs no approximation. Example: 9 of 20 convert against 2 of 20.

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: Chi-square, no correction

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: Chi-square with Yates' continuity correction

chunks.h: Proportions and counts: z, chi-square, Fisher, exact binomial
chunks.x: The expected counts here are 5.5, right at the edge, and the uncorrected chi-square's p-value (0.013) is less than half the exact one (0.031). For a single proportion against a fixed value, the exact binomial test plays the same role (the coin in section 05). Exact tests on counts are slightly conservative: the counts are whole numbers, so the achievable p-values jump and the real false-positive rate sits a little below alpha .
The Mann–Whitney U test (also called the Wilcoxon rank-sum test) ranks all observations together and compares the groups' rank sums. Equivalently, it counts how often a random B beats a random A:
beginaligned U &= \#\(b, a) : b gt a\ + tfrac12\, \#\(b, a) : b = a\ \\ fracUn_A n_B &approx P(B gt A) + tfrac12 P(B = A) endaligned

In words: U counts the pairs (one from each group) that B wins, with ties counting half, so U/(n_A n_B) is the share of pairs B wins. Formally the null is that the two distributions are identical; what the test detects is whether that share is far from ½, i.e. whether B tends to be larger. Only when one distribution is a shifted copy of the other does that amount to a shift in the median (and the mean); otherwise it tests neither. If the spreads differ, the Brunner–Munzel test targets P(B gt A) directly.

Where that bites. Revenue per user, where most users spend 0. A: 10% buy, and buyers' spend is lognormal ( sigma = 1 ) with mean 100. B: 11% buy, mean spend 80. Mean revenue per user is 10.0 for A and 8.8 for B, so B loses money. Simulated 200 times with 50,000 users per arm:
Welch's t on revenue per user: A is better, typical (median) p = 5 times 10^-5 .
Mann–Whitney: B is “better”, typical p = 6 times 10^-6 . Most pairs are zero against zero (ties); among the rest, B wins more often because it has more non-zero users.
In 98% of the runs both tests were significant, in opposite directions.

Both tests are right about their own question. The business question is total revenue, which is the mean, so the t-test is the relevant one. Choose the test by the quantity you want to make a decision about, then deal with the data's shape (section 04).

If the treatment changed nothing for anyone (the “sharp null”), each user's outcome would have been the same in either arm, so the group labels are arbitrary. Shuffle the labels many times, recompute the statistic each time, and see where the real one falls.

By hand. A: 3, 5, 4, 6 (mean 4.5). B: 7, 8, 6, 9 (mean 7.5). Observed difference 3.0. There are binom84 = 70 ways to split the eight values into two groups of four. Exactly 2 give a difference of +3.0 and 2 give −3.0, so the two-sided p = 4/70 = 0.057 . The t-test on the same numbers says p = 0.017 , but that leans on normality with four points per group. And no possible data could give this design a two-sided p below 2/70 = 0.029 .

When: small samples, any statistic (difference in medians, a ratio, a custom metric), odd distributions. Under random assignment it's exact, with no distributional assumption (this is called randomization inference).
The cost: computation, and its null is “identical distributions”, not just “equal means”. Shuffle the unit that was randomized: whole users, or whole clusters, never individual events.

To see how much a statistic would vary across samples, resample the data you have: draw n rows with replacement, compute the statistic, repeat a few thousand times. The spread of those values estimates the standard error; their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles give a percentile confidence interval. BCa (bias-corrected and accelerated) intervals adjust for skew and bias and are usually better.
When: intervals for medians, percentiles, ratios, differences of anything without a textbook formula.
Resample the independent unit: users, not page views; clusters, not members; blocks of time for time series.

Where it fails: very small samples (it can't see beyond the data); extremes such as the maximum; heavy tails, because it can't invent the whales the sample hasn't seen, so for a mean it's no better than the CLT; dependent data resampled as if independent.

Bootstrap vs permutation: the bootstrap estimates uncertainty around the data as they are (an interval); a permutation test asks how unusual the data are when the link between label and outcome is broken (a p-value).

Parametric tests (t, z) target a specific quantity, usually the mean, give an interval in the metric's own units, and have the most power when their assumptions hold. With large samples the CLT covers most of those assumptions.

Non-parametric tests (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon, sign test) assume less and resist outliers, but they test a different hypothesis (one group tends to be larger) and give effect sizes that are harder to turn into money.
Resampling methods (permutation, bootstrap) keep the quantity you care about and drop the distributional assumption, at the cost of computation.

Rule of thumb: for decisions about totals (revenue, orders), test means, with enough users and variance reduction. Use rank tests for ordinal data (ratings), small samples, or when “the typical user” is the question.

chunks.h: Assumptions, in order of how much they matter
chunks.x: Independence between the units analysed. The most important and the most often broken: page views of one user, users in one city, buyers sharing inventory. When it fails, the SE is too small and false positives soar (16% instead of 5% in the example in section 06), and no amount of data fixes it.

chunks.h: Assumptions, in order of how much they matter
chunks.x: The estimate is close to normal. Means of large samples are, thanks to the CLT, unless the metric is very skewed (section 04).

chunks.h: Assumptions, in order of how much they matter
chunks.x: Equal variances. Only Student's t needs it; use Welch.

chunks.h: Assumptions, in order of how much they matter
chunks.x: No interference between arms. One unit's treatment mustn't change another's outcome (section 06).

chunks.h: Why tests on means work for skewed metrics
chunks.x: The central limit theorem says that the average of n independent draws from any distribution with a finite variance sigma^2 is approximately normal for large n :

chunks.h: Why tests on means work for skewed metrics
chunks.x: beginaligned bar X &approx mathcal NBig(mu,\ fracsigma^2nBig) \\ SE(bar X) &= fracsigmasqrt n \\ SE(hat p) &= sqrtfracp(1-p)n endaligned

chunks.h: Why tests on means work for skewed metrics
chunks.x: In words: individual revenue can be wildly skewed, but the average over many users wobbles in a bell shape around the true mean, with a wobble that shrinks like 1/sqrt n . A t-test only needs the average to be normal, not the data.

chunks.h: Why tests on means work for skewed metrics
chunks.x: Three slips that come up under pressure. (1) “Revenue per user becomes normal with more users.” It never does; only the average does. (2) “The bell appears as the number of experiments grows.” It's the number of users per average, n , that matters. (3) SE = p(1-p)/sqrt n . The square root covers the whole variance: sqrtp(1-p)/n . For 10% at 10,000 users that's 0.003, so the 95% interval is ±0.59 points.

Skewness gamma = mathbb E[(X - mu)^3]/sigma^3 , the third standardized moment, measures lopsidedness: it's positive when a long tail stretches to the right. The skewness of a mean of n draws is gamma/sqrt n : averaging makes the shape more symmetric, but slowly. Two rules of thumb:
n ge 25gamma^2 makes the mean's own skewness at most 0.2, where the bell looks symmetric.
n ge 355gamma^2 is a stricter rule from online experimentation, meant to make the normal approximation good in the tails (where the test's decision happens), not just in the middle.
Lognormal spend, sigma = 1
Lognormal spend, sigma = 1.5
For conversion, gamma = (1 - 2p)/sqrtp(1-p) , so rarer events are more skewed. What goes wrong below these sizes: simulating a one-sample t-test of the true mean on exponential data ( gamma = 2 ):
False positives, low tail (2.5% nominal)

The errors are lopsided: with right-skewed data, a low sample mean tends to come with a low sample standard deviation, so the t statistic's low tail gets heavy. One-sided tests suffer most, and “ n ge 30 ” is only safe for mild skew.

Two-sample tests are more forgiving. In a balanced A/A test both arms share the same skew, and it largely cancels in the difference: with 30 users per arm, each tail is 2.5%. Skew still bites one-sample tests, unbalanced splits (270 against 30 users: 5.6% low, 0.9% high), and intervals when the treatment changes the shape of the distribution.

chunks.h: Heavy tails: when the variance explodes
chunks.x: Some metrics have a few enormous values that carry much of the total: revenue (whales), order sizes, session lengths, claim amounts. Two things go wrong.

chunks.h: Heavy tails: when the variance explodes
chunks.x: The sample hasn't seen the tail yet. For lognormal data with sigma = 2 the true standard deviation is 54, but a typical (median) sample of 1,000 shows about 31, and 85% of such samples come in below 54: the rare giants that make up most of the variance usually haven't been drawn yet. The estimated SE is too small and the test is overconfident.

chunks.h: Heavy tails: when the variance explodes
chunks.x: The variance may not exist. For a Pareto distribution with tail index 1.5 the mean is finite but the variance is infinite. The sample standard deviation never settles: its typical value grows from about 6 at n = 1,000 to 9, 15 and 23 at 10,000, 100,000 and a million, and keeps growing. The usual CLT doesn't apply; averages converge more slowly and jump whenever a new giant arrives.

chunks.h: Heavy tails: when the variance explodes
chunks.x: A realistic whale metric. 5% of users buy; spend per buyer is lognormal with median about 55 and sigma = 1.5 . Revenue per user then has mean 8.4, standard deviation 115 (a coefficient of variation of 14) and skewness about 130. The top 1% of users bring 75% of the revenue, the top 0.1% bring 30%. Detecting a true 10% lift with 80% power needs about 296,000 users per arm.

chunks.x: about 5%: no better than chance

chunks.h: The fixes, and the question each one answers
chunks.x: Capping at the 99.9th percentile (about 1,200) lowers the mean by 15% but the variance by 72%. The lift measured on the capped metric is 8.3% rather than 10%, because the cap clips some of the treatment's biggest gains, yet power rises from about a third to more than half. Under H_0 both arms are capped identically, so the test stays valid; what changes is the quantity being estimated.

chunks.h: The fixes, and the question each one answers
chunks.x: The log answers a different question. For A = 1, 1, 1, 1000 and B = 10, 10, 10, 10, the means are 250.75 and 10, but the mean log_10 is 0.75 against 1.0 (geometric means 5.6 against 10). The log says B wins; revenue says A wins by 25×. On zero-heavy data, log(1 + x) also mixes “bought or not” with “how much”.

chunks.h: The fixes, and the question each one answers
chunks.x: Trimming 10% from each end removes the bottom 10% (zeros) and the top 10%, which contains all the buyers when only 5% buy. Both trimmed means are 0, so the test can never reject.

chunks.h: The fixes, and the question each one answers
chunks.x: Mann–Whitney sees mostly zero-against-zero ties, so it is essentially testing conversion, which the treatment didn't change; among buyers, a treatment buyer outspends a control buyer only 51.8% of the time.

chunks.h: The fixes, and the question each one answers
chunks.x: Choosing the cap after seeing the results. Different caps give different p-values, and picking the best one is p-hacking. Fix the cap in the analysis plan, from pre-experiment data or as a pooled percentile, and report the uncapped result alongside.
For latency, “the median got faster” or “p90 got faster” is often the real question. The standard error of a sample quantile at level q is approximately:
SE(hat x_q) approx frac1f(x_q) sqrtfracq(1 - q)n

In words: f(x_q) is the density at that quantile. Where data are sparse (the tail), the quantile is poorly pinned down. For normal data the median's SE is 1.25\,sigma/sqrt n , 25% noisier than the mean; for exponential data with mean 1, the 90th percentile's SE is 3/sqrt n . Because the density is unknown, test quantiles with a bootstrap over the randomized unit (users, not requests, since one user's requests are correlated) or with quantile regression and clustered standard errors.

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: Under H_0 (a fair coin), the number of heads X is binomial with n = 100 , p = 0.5 : mean np = 50 , standard deviation sqrtnp(1-p) = 5 .

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: beginaligned z &= frac80 - 505 = 6 \\ p_normal &= 2\,big(1 - Phi(6)big) approx 2 times 10^-9 \\ p_exact &= 2\,P(X ge 80) approx 1.1 times 10^-9 endaligned

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: In words: 80 heads is six standard deviations from what a fair coin gives. Both the normal approximation and the exact binomial say the coin is biased beyond reasonable doubt. A 95% interval for the coin's heads rate is 0.8 pm 1.96 times 0.04 = [0.72, 0.88] (the Wilson interval, better near 0 or 1, gives [0.71, 0.87]); it's nowhere near 0.5.

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: The interesting case is the borderline one. 60 heads in 100:

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: Normal with continuity correction

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: The continuity correction: the count is a whole number, so “60 or more” starts at 59.5 on a continuous scale. Using 59.5 brings the normal approximation almost exactly onto the exact answer.

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: The exact cut-off: a fair coin is rejected at 5% for 61 or more heads, or 39 or fewer. Because counts jump in whole steps, that rule's actual false-positive rate is 3.5%, not 5%.

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: Small n : 8 heads in 10 gives an exact p = 0.11 while the normal approximation says 0.058. With np = 5 the approximation is poor; use the exact test.

chunks.h: Is the coin biased? 80 heads in 100 tosses
chunks.x: Power: to detect a coin that lands heads 55% of the time with 80% power, you need about 783 tosses.
For 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 200 the mean is 31.9 and the median is 4. Right skew pulls the mean above the median.
The mean is what adds up: mean revenue × users = total revenue. It's what finance cares about, and it's sensitive to every extreme.
The median describes the typical unit and ignores extremes, but it doesn't add up (the median of a sum isn't the sum of medians), and its standard error needs the density or a bootstrap.
Which to test follows from the decision: totals mean the mean; experience of a typical user (latency, delivery time) often means the median or a percentile.

chunks.h: The coefficient of variation, and sample size in relative terms
chunks.x: The coefficient of variation is CV = sigma/mu , the spread in units of the mean. Divide the sample-size formula's top and bottom by mu^2 and write the MDE as a relative lift r = delta/mu :

chunks.h: The coefficient of variation, and sample size in relative terms
chunks.x: beginaligned n &approx frac16\,sigma^2delta^2 = frac16\,(sigma/mu)^2(delta/mu)^2 = frac16\,CV^2r^2 \\ CV_conversion &= sqrtfrac1 - pp endaligned

chunks.h: The coefficient of variation, and sample size in relative terms
chunks.x: In words: the users you need depend only on how noisy the metric is relative to its level, and on the relative lift you want to see. Examples:

chunks.h: The coefficient of variation, and sample size in relative terms
chunks.x: Conversion at 10% (CV = 3), +8% relative: 16 times 9 / 0.08^2 = 22,500 per arm, the same as before.

chunks.h: The coefficient of variation, and sample size in relative terms
chunks.x: Conversion at 1% (CV ≈ 9.95), +5% relative: 633,600 per arm. Rare events need far more users for the same relative lift.

chunks.h: The coefficient of variation, and sample size in relative terms
chunks.x: Revenue with CV 5, +2% relative: 1,000,000 per arm. The whale metric (CV ≈ 14) at +10% needs about 300,000.

chunks.h: Normals under shift, scale and sums
chunks.x: beginaligned X sim mathcal N(mu, sigma^2) \;&Rightarrow\; aX + b sim mathcal N(amu + b,\ a^2sigma^2) \\ X + Y &sim mathcal N(mu_X + mu_Y,\ sigma_X^2 + sigma_Y^2) \\ X - Y &sim mathcal N(mu_X - mu_Y,\ sigma_X^2 + sigma_Y^2) \\ bar X_n &sim mathcal N(mu,\ sigma^2/n) \\ Var(X pm Y) &= sigma_X^2 + sigma_Y^2 pm 2rho\,sigma_Xsigma_Y endaligned

chunks.h: Normals under shift, scale and sums
chunks.x: In words: shifting moves the mean; scaling multiplies the mean and multiplies the standard deviation by lvert a rvert (the variance by a^2 ); the result is still normal. Sums and differences of independent normals are normal, and their variances add either way, which is why the SE of a difference between two arms is sqrtSE_A^2 + SE_B^2 . The last line (it holds for any distributions) is where correlation enters, and it's the reason pairing and CUPED work.

Two means, 10 and 13, each with SE 1. Their 95% intervals are [8.04, 11.96] and [11.04, 14.96]: they overlap. But the difference has SE = sqrt1 + 1 = 1.41 , so z = 3/1.41 = 2.12 and p = 0.034 : significant.

In words: two intervals only fail to overlap when the gap exceeds 1.96 times (1 + 1) = 3.92 , but significance needs only 1.96 times 1.41 = 2.77 , because standard errors combine by the square root of summed squares, not by adding. Intervals that just touch correspond to p approx 0.006 . Compare the interval of the difference, not two separate intervals.

The statistics of an A/B test are the two-sample test from section 03. Almost everything that goes wrong in practice is upstream of it: the wrong metric, the wrong unit, broken assignment, a test that stopped too early, or arms that leak into each other. The steps below are in the order you'd plan them.

chunks.h: 1. Choose the metric before anything else
chunks.x: The overall evaluation criterion (OEC): the one metric (or a fixed weighted combination) that decides shipping. It should move within the test's duration and predict long-term value: orders per user, retained users, revenue per user.

chunks.h: 1. Choose the metric before anything else
chunks.x: Guardrails: metrics that must not get worse: latency, crash rate, refunds, unsubscribes, complaints. Plus trust guardrails that check the experiment itself, such as the sample ratio (step 5).

chunks.h: 1. Choose the metric before anything else
chunks.x: Sensitivity vs directionality. A sensitive metric moves detectably when something changes (clicks); a directional metric moves the way long-term value moves (retention, revenue). Clicks are sensitive but can be gamed by clickbait; revenue is directional but noisy. The usual compromise is a sensitive metric that has been checked against long-term outcomes in past experiments.

chunks.h: 1. Choose the metric before anything else
chunks.x: The form of the metric matters for the maths: a per-user mean (revenue per user), a proportion of users (converted or not), or a ratio of totals (clicks per page view). Ratios need the delta method (step 2).

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: The unit of randomization is what gets assigned to an arm: a user, a session, a device, a page view, a city. The unit of analysis is what the metric averages over. The rule: analyse at the unit you randomized, or correct the standard error.

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: Most product changes; consistent experience

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: Logged-out traffic; one person on several devices

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: Cookies reset; one person can land in both arms

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: Invisible back-end changes (ranking latency); many more units

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: A user sees both versions; learning effects carry over

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: Cluster (city, store, driver pool)

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: Interference between users (step 9)

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: Few units, so wide intervals

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: The SE mistake. Randomize by user, then compute click-through rate as clicks / page views and test it as if every page view were an independent coin flip. Page views of one user are correlated (some users click a lot, some never), so the effective sample is much smaller than the number of page views and the naive SE is too small.

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: The fix: the delta method. Work with per-user totals: Y_i clicks and X_i page views for user i , n users per arm. The metric is a ratio of means, hat R = bar Y / bar X . A first-order Taylor expansion around the true means gives

chunks.x: beginaligned hat R - R &approx fracbar Y - mu_Ymu_X - fracmu_Y\,(bar X - mu_X)mu_X^2 \\ Var(hat R) &approx frac1n\,mu_X^2Big(sigma_Y^2 - 2R\,sigma_XY + R^2sigma_X^2Big) endaligned

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: In words: the ratio wobbles when clicks wobble and when page views wobble, and the covariance term matters because heavy users have more of both. Every quantity is a per-user mean, variance or covariance, so the users are the independent units, as randomized.
