chunks.x: Gradient boosting and XGBoost · Deepam Minda

Boosting builds F(x) = F_0 + eta sum_m f_m(x) , one small regression tree at a time. Each tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions: the residual y - F for squared error, y - p for log loss. It's gradient descent, with each step a tree.

A leaf stores a correction, not a target. For squared error the best correction is the mean residual and the best split is the biggest drop in squared error. For classification F is the log-odds, and the sigmoid is applied once, to the total.

XGBoost expands each row's loss to second order around its current prediction: slope g and bend h . Summing over a leaf gives the best leaf value w^* = -G/(H + lambda) . A split's gain is half of (left score + right score − parent score), minus gamma , where a node's score is G^2/(H + lambda) . For log loss, g = p - y and h = p(1 - p) .

lambda shrinks leaves with a small hessian sum (few rows, or rows the model is already sure about), gamma is a price per leaf, and min_child_weight is a minimum hessian per child. All three stop a leaf chasing a handful of rows.

Missing values: at every split, the missing rows' G and H are tried on the left and on the right, and the better side is stored as the default direction. If training had no missing values, that direction was never learned.

Speed comes from histograms (bin once, sum g and h per bin, get one child by subtraction) and parallel work inside each tree. LightGBM adds leaf-wise growth, GOSS and EFB; CatBoost adds ordered target statistics, ordered boosting and symmetric trees.

Boosting cuts bias and overfits as trees are added; a forest cuts variance and doesn't. Fix eta , early-stop on a validation set that looks like production, then tune depth and min_child_weight, subsampling, and the penalties.

In practice: scale_pos_weight multiplies the predicted odds (recalibrate), monotone constraints are enforced at split time with bounds on the leaf values, split-count and gain importances mislead (prefer SHAP), and a sum of trees can't extrapolate.

Six loan applicants and one feature: how many late payments they've had. The same rows carry two targets: a credit limit for regression (section 02) and whether they defaulted for classification (section 05).
Watch row 3. It defaulted with 0 late payments, just like rows 1 and 2, who didn't. No question about late payments can separate it from them, so it shows what boosting does with a row it can't fix.
Settings used throughout: learning rate eta = 0.3 (XGBoost's default), and each tree makes one split, so every tree can be worked by hand. The same steps work at any depth.
A tree is questions plus numbers

A tree asks a few yes/no questions, like “late < 1.5?”, to send each row to a leaf, and each leaf holds one number. Building a tree means choosing two things: the questions, which decide which rows end up together, and the number in each leaf. A row the tree has never seen still falls into some leaf, so the tree works on new data too.
The model is a sum of trees
F(x) = F_0 + eta\, f_1(x) + dots + eta\, f_M(x)
F_0 is the starting number, the same for everyone.
f_m(x) is the m -th tree's output: a correction to the prediction so far, not a prediction on its own.
eta is the learning rate: each correction is only partly trusted (section 02 says why).
For regression, F is the prediction itself. For classification, F is a score, the log-odds, which becomes a probability only at the very end (section 05).
One loss for the whole model

Each row gets a penalty for how wrong it is, and the penalties add up: L = sum_i ell(y_i, F_i) . For regression ell = tfrac12 (y - F)^2 , so being off by 10 costs 50; for classification it's the log loss. Everything below is chosen to make this one number smaller: the starting number, every split and every leaf.

Choosing 100 trees at once to minimize L is hopeless: there are far too many combinations. So boosting is greedy (the textbook name is forward stagewise additive modelling): keep everything built so far fixed, find the one new tree that lowers L the most, add it, freeze it, repeat. Every round solves the same problem: with the current predictions F_i fixed, find the tree f that minimizes
sum_i ellbig(y_i,\ F_i + f(x_i)big)

This is “the loss inside the tree”. It isn't Gini or entropy, which belong to a standalone classification tree; it's the model's own loss, measured after adding the new tree. And since a leaf holds a number to be added, every tree in boosting is a regression tree, even for classification.
Boosting vs a random forest
Independently, each on a bootstrap sample
One after another, each fixing the last
Shallow, typically depth 3–8
Variance: jumpy deep trees, averaged
Bias: weak trees, added up
Never hurts; validation loss goes flat
Eventually overfits; needs early stopping

In an interview: “Boosting builds an additive model, a starting value plus a sum of small trees. Each tree is a correction to the prediction so far, fitted greedily to lower one loss given everything before it. Each is a regression tree, even for classification, because its leaves hold numbers that get added to a score. A forest averages independent deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees in sequence to cut bias, which is why it can overfit as trees are added.”
The loss is tfrac12 (y - F)^2 . Every step asks one question: what makes this loss smallest?
Round 0: the starting number
Before any tree exists, which single number c should everyone get? Try a few:
Total loss tfrac12sum (y - c)^2
The bottom is at 80, the mean. In general the slope of tfrac12sum (y - c)^2 in c is sum (c - y) , which is zero at c = bar y . So F_0 = 80 for every row.
Tree 1: the number in a leaf
What's left to fix for each row is its residual, r = y - F :
Suppose a leaf holds rows 1–4. Every row in it gets the same nudge w . Which w makes these rows' loss smallest? After the nudge, the leaf's loss is
sum_leaf tfrac12big(y_i - (F_i + w)big)^2 = sum_leaf tfrac12 (r_i - w)^2
The bottom is at 15, the mean residual. Setting the slope -sum (r_i - w) to zero gives it in general:
w^* = frac1n_leaf sum_leaf r_i
Residuals aren't a trick someone made up. They fall straight out of asking which nudge makes squared error smallest.
A leaf stores a correction, not a target. Rows 1–4 have a mean limit of 95, but the leaf stores +15, because 80 + 15 = 95.
Tree 1: choosing the split

Which question should the tree ask? The one that leaves the least loss, once each side gets its best nudge. Before any split the node's best nudge is the mean residual, 0, so the loss is tfrac12sum r^2 = 1600 .

The winning 250: left residuals 20, 30, 10, 0 minus 15 are 5, 15, −5, −15, whose squares add to 500; the right residuals −30, −30 minus −30 are 0. Half of 500 is 250, and the drop is 1600 − 250 = 1350. Tree 1 is “late < 1.5? → +15, otherwise −30”: an ordinary regression tree, grown on residuals instead of on y .
A shortcut you'll see again. The drop needs only sums and counts:
beginaligned drop &= frac12 Big[ frac(sum r_L)^2n_L + frac(sum r_R)^2n_R \\ &qquad - frac(sum r)^2n Big] endaligned

For late < 1.5: ½ × [60²/4 + (−60)²/2 − 0²/6] = ½ × [900 + 1800] = 1350. It works because giving a group its mean residual removes exactly tfrac12 (sum r)^2/n of its loss: (sum)²/count is big when many rows push the same way. XGBoost's gain (section 06) is exactly this with new names.
Deeper trees repeat the search inside each child, on that child's rows only, with that child's own loss as the “before”. They stop at the maximum depth, or when no split lowers the loss.
Don't add the whole tree. Add eta times it, with eta = 0.3 : +4.5 for rows 1–4 and −9 for rows 5–6, so F becomes 84.5 (rows 1–4) and 71 (rows 5–6).

Why not the full +15 and −30? Tree 1 was fitted to these exact rows, noise included, so trusting it fully overfits. Taking 30% leaves room for later trees to correct it. The cost is more trees (section 03).

Does eta change which split wins? No. The split search pretends the full leaf value will be added; eta is applied afterwards. Adding only eta of a leaf's value removes a share 2eta - eta^2 of its full drop (expand tfrac12sum (r - eta w)^2 ). With eta = 0.3 that's 0.51 for every split: 1200 → 612, 1350 → 688.5, 540 → 275.4. Every drop shrinks by the same factor, so the order is unchanged. What eta does change is the residuals the next tree sees.
Every residual is now measured against the current prediction, r = y - F_0 - eta f_1(x) :
Tree 2 does exactly what Tree 1 did, on these residuals. The loss before any split is ½Σr² = 911.5.

The best split moved. Tree 1 pushed row 4 (limit 80) up to 84.5, so it's now over-predicted ( r = -4.5 ) and belongs with the “push down” group. Each tree sees only what's left over, so different trees cut in different places, and their sum builds a staircase.

Trap: average the residuals, not the targets. In Tree 1 you couldn't tell them apart, because every row had the same F . Now you can. On the right side of late < 0.5 (rows 4–6, with F = 84.5, 71, 71), the mean target is 60: as a nudge, that would send row 4 from 84.5 to 144.5. The mean residual is −15.5, which moves each row toward its target, leaving a loss of ½ × (11² + 5.5² + 5.5²) = 90.75.
Tree 2 is “late < 0.5? → +15.5, otherwise −15.5”. Times eta , that's ±4.65, so F becomes 89.15 (late 0), 79.85 (late 1) and 66.35 (late 2–3).
Where it ends, and predicting a new row
The six rows (dots) and the prediction after 0, 1, 2 and 50 trees. Tree 1 cuts at 1.5, tree 2 at 0.5; after 50 trees the staircase sits at the mean limit for each number of late payments.
It settles at the mean limit for each number of late payments: (100 + 110 + 90)/3 = 100, then 80, then 50. That's the best squared error can do with this one feature.
A new applicant with 2 late payments, after 2 trees: add up the start and each tree's shrunk leaf value.
beginaligned F &= 80 + 0.3 times (-30) + 0.3 times (-15.5) \\ &= 80 - 9 - 4.65 \\ &= 66.35 endaligned

With 1 late payment: 80 + 4.5 − 4.65 = 79.85. Tree 1 sends late = 1 left, but Tree 2 sends it right. For regression, the sum is the prediction. And an applicant with 10 late payments also gets 66.35: past the last split, a sum of trees is flat (section 13).
The regression loop in one box

F0 = mean(y) F = F0 for every row repeat for each tree: r = y - F # what's left per row split: biggest drop in ½Σr² # each side gets its mean r leaf value = mean r of its rows F = F + eta * (row's leaf value) predict(x) = F0 + eta * Σ (x's leaf values)

In an interview: “Start from the mean. Each round computes residuals against the current prediction and fits a small regression tree to them: the leaf value is the mean residual, the split is the biggest drop in squared error, and the tree goes in after shrinking by the learning rate. Leaves store corrections, not targets; from the second tree on, rows in a leaf have different predictions, so you average residuals, not targets.”
The slope of tfrac12 (y - F)^2 in the prediction F is F - y . So the residual is minus the slope:
beginaligned fracpartialpartial F\, tfrac12 (y - F)^2 &= F - y \\ r &= y - F \\ &= -fracpartialpartial F\, tfrac12 (y - F)^2 endaligned

Each tree in section 02 was fitted to minus the slope of every row's loss: the downhill direction for that row. Adding the tree moves every row a little way downhill. That's gradient descent, and it generalizes to any loss you can differentiate.
Gradient descent on the predictions
Treat the n training predictions as the parameters. Their loss is a function of n numbers, and plain gradient descent would update each one:
beginaligned L(F_1, dots, F_n) &= sum_i ell(y_i, F_i) \\ g_i &= fracpartial ell(y_i, F_i)partial F_i \\ F_i &leftarrow F_i - eta\, g_i endaligned

That would just memorize the training rows, and say nothing about a new x . So boosting replaces the step -g by the tree that's closest to it, which is a function of the features and therefore works for any row:
beginaligned f_m &= argmin_f in trees sum_i big(-g_i - f(x_i)big)^2 \\ F_m(x) &= F_m-1(x) + eta\, f_m(x) endaligned

In words: the tree is the best tree-shaped approximation of the negative gradient, and adding it is one gradient step taken in the space of functions. That's why it's called functional gradient descent, and why -g_i is called the pseudo-residual.
Friedman's algorithm (classic gradient boosting)
Start at the best constant: F_0 = argmin_c sum_i ell(y_i, c) .
Each round: compute the pseudo-residuals r_i = -g_i at F_m-1 .
Fit a regression tree to the r_i by squared error. This only chooses the regions (the leaves).
Re-set each leaf to the value that minimizes the real loss on that leaf's rows: c_j = argmin_c sum_i in j ellbig(y_i, F_m-1(x_i) + cbig) .
Add eta times the tree, and repeat.
y - F , capped at pmdelta
Close to a mean that ignores the extremes
One Newton step (section 05)
Log-odds of the base rate

Why step 4 matters. For absolute error the tree is fitted to signs, ±1, so its raw leaf values are at most 1 in size: useless as step sizes when the residuals are in the tens. Re-setting each leaf to its median residual makes every step the right size. For squared error the mean residual is already the best value, so step 4 changes nothing. For log loss the best value has no formula, so it takes one Newton step instead. XGBoost goes further and uses that Newton information to choose the splits too (section 06).

Why the loss matters: outliers. In a larger simulated loan book, corrupting 2% of the training limits with a +₹500k typo gave a test RMSE of 29.0 under squared error, against 10.5 under absolute error and 10.9 under Huber. Under squared error those rows have residuals near 500 and every tree chases them; under absolute error each row only says “up” or “down”.

F_0 is the best constant for the loss: the mean for squared error, the median for absolute error, and the log-odds of the base rate for log loss, where the slope sum (p - y) is zero exactly when p = bar y . A bad start isn't fatal but wastes trees: in the same simulated book (8.7% defaults), starting XGBoost at p = 0.5 needed 64 trees instead of 35 to reach the same test log loss, because the first trees spent themselves walking everyone down to 8.7%. Recent XGBoost versions estimate the start from the data for this reason.
Shrinkage: why a small learning rate generalizes better

Each tree is a greedy, noisy estimate of the downhill direction, fitted to the same rows it will be judged on. A full step bakes all of that noise in, and later trees have to spend themselves undoing it. A small step keeps only a little of each tree, so the final model is an average over many trees, each fitted to slightly different residuals: the noise in any one of them is diluted. It's the same reason a small step size makes gradient descent stable. Validation log loss on the simulated book, depth-3 trees, 400 trees each:
A large rate overshoots: best after 2 trees, and a worse best.

Small rates trade off with the number of trees: for the two small rates, eta times trees is about the same (0.03 × 91 ≈ 0.01 × 266 ≈ 2.7), because small steps walk roughly the same path in shorter strides.
A small rate forgives a bad tree count: past the best round it climbs slowly (0.233 after 400 trees at 0.01) where a large one climbs fast (0.280 at 0.1).
The cost is training and prediction time, both proportional to the number of trees.
Stochastic gradient boosting

Friedman's later variant fits each tree on a random subsample of the rows, drawn without replacement, typically 50–80% (subsample). The tree is then applied to every row, so every prediction still moves. It helps in three ways: consecutive trees can't all latch onto the same noisy rows, so they're less alike and the sum has lower variance; each tree is cheaper; and the left-out rows give a free out-of-bag estimate of each round's improvement. The cost is a little bias and noisier steps, so it usually wants a few more trees. Column subsampling (section 09) does the same with features.

In an interview: “Gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space. Each round computes the negative gradient of the loss for every row at the current predictions, fits a regression tree to it by least squares, sets each leaf to the value that minimizes the real loss there, and adds a shrunk copy. For squared error the negative gradient is the residual, so ‘fit the residuals’ is a special case; for absolute error it's the sign; for log loss it's y - p . Start at the best constant, keep the learning rate small, and subsample rows to decorrelate the trees.”

chunks.h: g and h: the same thing, renamed
chunks.x: Section 02 used residuals and row counts, which only make sense for squared error. This section renames them so the same steps work for any loss. Nothing new happens yet.

chunks.x: For every row define g = F - y (minus the residual) and h = 1 . Over the rows of a leaf, G = sum g , which is -sum r , and H = sum h , which is the row count n . Section 02's two results become:

chunks.x: Why these names? Nudge a leaf by w . From section 02 the slope of the leaf's loss is -sum (r - w) , which is

chunks.x: Read it like walking down a hill. G is the slope right now, at w = 0 : its sign says which way is downhill and its size how steep. H is how fast that slope flattens per unit walked. If the slope is G and it flattens by H per unit, you reach flat ground after G/H units downhill: w = -G/H . On Tree 1's left leaf ( G = -60 , H = 4 ):

chunks.h: g and h: the same thing, renamed
chunks.x: So per row, g is the slope of that row's loss in its prediction (the gradient), and h is the bend, how fast the slope changes (the hessian, the second derivative). For squared error the slope is F - y and the bend is always 1, which is why section 02 looked like “mean residual”. “Residual” and “row count” only mean something for squared error; “slope” and “bend” mean something for any loss with two derivatives and a bend above 0. Section 05 swaps in log loss and keeps every step.

chunks.h: g and h: the same thing, renamed
chunks.x: In an interview: “Write g for each row's gradient of the loss with respect to its prediction and h for the second derivative. For squared error g = F - y and h = 1 , so -G/H is the mean residual and the gain is the squared-error drop.”
F is a score, and the sigmoid comes last

A sum of trees can be any number, while a probability must stay in (0, 1), and probabilities can't be added (0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3). So for classification F is the log-odds, and it becomes a probability only at the very end:
beginaligned p &= sigma(F) \\ &= frac11 + e^-F \\ F &= logfracp1 - p endaligned
A tree has no sigmoid inside it. Each leaf holds a change in log-odds, like −0.3 or +0.6.
The sigmoid is applied once, to the total: p = sigma(F_0 + eta f_1 + eta f_2 + dots) .
During training the sigmoid appears only when computing g and h , always on the running total F .
ell = -big[\, y log p + (1 - y) log (1 - p) \,big]

A defaulter costs -log p and a non-defaulter -log(1 - p) : a defaulter given p = 0.9, 0.5 or 0.1 costs 0.11, 0.69 or 2.30. The best single probability for everyone is the base rate, here 3/6 = 0.5, so F_0 = log(0.5/0.5) , which is 0, and every row starts at p = 0.5 . In general F_0 = logfracbar y1 - bar y ; for a 10% default rate that's log(0.1/0.9) = -2.20 .
The slope g and the bend h
One fact does all the work: the sigmoid's slope is p(1 - p) .
beginaligned fracdsigmadF &= frace^-F(1 + e^-F)^2 \\ &= frac11 + e^-F cdot frace^-F1 + e^-F \\ &= p\,(1 - p) endaligned
The slope g , by the chain rule through p :
beginaligned y = 1:quad fracdelldF &= -frac1p cdot p(1 - p) \\ &= p - 1 \\ y = 0:quad fracdelldF &= frac11 - p cdot p(1 - p) \\ &= p \\ both:quad g &= p - y endaligned
The bend h : in g = p - y only p moves as F moves, at the sigmoid's rate, so
beginaligned h &= fracdgdF \\ &= p\,(1 - p) endaligned
g = p - y is the probability error, with a sign. Positive means p is too high, so push down. It plays the role the residual played ( y - p = -g ).
h = p(1 - p) is how much p moves when F moves by 1. It depends on how sure the model already is: 0.25 at p = 0.5 , 0.09 at 0.9, 0.0099 at 0.99.

This is the one real difference from regression: h is no longer 1. A row the model is unsure about has a large h ; a row it's sure about has h near 0. And the claim about round 0 follows: for a single constant the slope is sum (p - y) , zero at p = bar y .
Why the exact leaf value doesn't work
In section 02 each leaf's best nudge was exact. Try that here, on the split late < 1.5:
Left leaf (rows 1–4, labels 0, 0, 1, 0, all at F = 0 ): the best probability is the leaf's rate, 1/4, so the best nudge solves sigma(0 + w) = 1/4 : w = log(1/3) , about −1.10. That one works.
Right leaf (rows 5–6, both defaulted): the best probability is 1, so w = +infty . A pure leaf wants infinity.

From Tree 2 on, rows in a leaf have different F s, and the best w solves sum_i sigma(F_i + w) = sum_i y_i , which has no formula. A numerical search for every leaf of every candidate split, every round, is too slow, and each new loss would need its own solver.
The shortcut: a Newton step
Do exactly what section 04 did: the slope is G now and it flattens by H per unit, so walk G/H downhill.
beginaligned w &= -fracGH \\ &= -fracsum_i (p_i - y_i)sum_i p_i (1 - p_i) endaligned
For squared error this is exact, because the bend really is constant.

For log loss it's an approximation. As you walk, p shifts and the bend changes; we pretend it stays at today's value. That replaces each row's loss curve with a parabola with the same slope and bend at the current point: the second-order approximation, or a Newton step (step = −slope / bend). It's close enough, and the next tree corrects what's left.
On Tree 1's leaves: left, G = 1 , H = 1 , so w = -1 (exact: −1.10); right, G = -1 , H = 0.5 , so w = +2 (exact: ∞, but the shortcut gives a finite step).

Why divide by H , not by the number of rows? g is an error in probability, while F is measured in log-odds. Near p = 0.5 , one unit of log-odds moves p by about 0.25. The left leaf is 0.25 too high on average, so it needs about 0.25 / 0.25 = 1 unit down. Dividing by h converts “wrong in probability” into “how far to move in log-odds”. In regression F and y share units, so h = 1 .

The split score carries over unchanged: the same tfrac12[G_L^2/H_L + G_R^2/H_R - G^2/H] , now the loss a split removes under the parabola. It's Newton's method for logistic regression, one leaf at a time.
Every row is at p = 0.5 , so g = 0.5 - y and h = 0.25 :
The whole node has G = 0 , H = 1.5 . Each cut:

For late < 1.5: ½ × [1²/1 + (−1)²/0.5 − 0²/1.5] = ½ × [1 + 2] = 1.5. Why the parent scores 0: G = 0 . Half the rows want to go up and half down, so one shared nudge helps no one. A split earns its gain by letting the two sides move in opposite directions.

Leaves: −1/1 = −1 and 1/0.5 = +2. Times eta = 0.3 : F becomes −0.3 for rows 1–4 and +0.6 for rows 5–6, so p = 0.426 and 0.646. (Added in full, the step would give 0.27 and 0.88 after one tree: very confident, on two rows.)
Recompute g and h at the new F . The parabola fits only near where you're standing, so you measure again every round.
Rows 5–6 push less ( g : −0.5 → −0.354). They've been partly fixed.
Row 3's g grew (−0.5 → −0.574). Tree 1 pushed it the wrong way, because it shares a leaf with two non-defaulters, and no split on “late” can ever pull it out.
Splits: late < 0.5 scores 0.11, late < 1.5 scores 0.80, late < 2.5 scores 0.32.
Leaves (from unrounded sums): left G = 0.7022 , H = 0.9778 , value −0.7181; right G = -0.7087 , H = 0.4576 , value +1.5488.
Times eta : −0.215 and +0.465, so F becomes −0.515 ( p = 0.374) for rows 1–4 and +1.065 ( p = 0.744) for rows 5–6. The steps shrink (+0.6 → +0.465 on the right) because the errors shrink.
Where it ends, and predicting a new row
Late 0 settles at 1/3, the real default rate in that group (row 3 of rows 1–3), and the best possible, since row 3 can't be separated.

Late 1 and late 2–3 head to 0 and 1. By 200 trees their scores are F = -16.1 and +17.6 : “certain”, on one and two rows. That's overfitting in miniature: pure groups keep pulling their F toward ±∞. XGBoost's lambda slows it (with lambda = 1 the late 2–3 score after 200 trees is 3.9, not 17.6), and early stopping stops it.
A new applicant with 2 late payments, after 2 trees: add the log-odds, then apply the sigmoid once.
beginaligned F &= 0 + 0.6 + 0.465 \\ &= 1.065 \\ p &= sigma(1.065) \\ &= 0.744 endaligned

The algorithm is identical in both columns; only the formulas for g and h change. Multiclass works the same way with K scores per row: each round grows K trees, one per class, on g_k = p_k - y_k with p_k from the softmax (each class uses only its own h_k ; the cross-class terms of the hessian are ignored), so 100 rounds with 3 classes is 300 trees.

In an interview: “For classification F is the log-odds and p = sigma(F) . Trees add log-odds corrections and the sigmoid is applied once, to the sum. Log loss has g = p - y and h = p(1 - p) , both from the sigmoid's slope. There's no closed-form best leaf value, and a pure leaf would want infinity, so each leaf takes a Newton step, -G/H : total gradient over total curvature. Dividing by h converts a probability error into a step in log-odds.”

Section 05 already did XGBoost's core: it chose splits and leaf values from g and h . On top of that, XGBoost adds penalties inside the objective (this section and 07), a learned direction for missing values (08), and engineering for speed (09).

Why it needs penalties. Look at the right leaf in section 05: +2 in Tree 1 and +1.55 in Tree 2, each time from just two rows, and a score of 17.6 after 200 trees. Small leaves take big swings on very little evidence. So XGBoost minimizes the loss plus a price for complexity:
beginaligned Obj &= sum_i ellbig(y_i,\ F_i + f(x_i)big) \\ &quad + gamma T + tfrac12 lambda sum_j=1^T w_j^2 endaligned
In words: the loss after adding this round's tree f , plus gamma for each of its T leaves, plus an L2 price lambda on its leaf values w_j (the same idea as ridge regression).
The derivation in five steps

Step 1: the objective is the line above. Step 2: replace each row's loss with a parabola. A Taylor expansion approximates a curve near a point from its value, slope and bend there; “second order” means stopping at the bend. The tree nudges row i by f_i = f(x_i) :
beginaligned ell(y_i,\ F_i + f_i) &approx ell(y_i, F_i) + g_i f_i + tfrac12 h_i f_i^2 \\ g_i &= fracpartial ell(y_i, F_i)partial F_i \\ h_i &= fracpartial^2 ell(y_i, F_i)partial F_i^2 endaligned

In words: loss after the nudge ≈ loss now + slope × nudge + ½ × bend × nudge². Why second order: a first-order version ( g f alone) is a straight line, which has no bottom: it says which way is downhill, not how far. The bend makes it a parabola, and a parabola's bottom has a formula.
Step 3: group the rows by leaf. Every row in leaf j gets the same w_j . Drop ell(y_i, F_i) , which the tree can't change, and add up each leaf's rows:
beginaligned Obj &approx sum_j=1^T Big[\, G_j w_j + tfrac12 (H_j + lambda)\, w_j^2 \,Big] + gamma T \\ G_j &= sum_i in j g_i \\ H_j &= sum_i in j h_i endaligned
Each leaf is now its own parabola, and lambda simply adds to the bend.
Step 4: the best leaf value. Set each leaf's slope to zero:
beginaligned G_j + (H_j + lambda)\, w_j &= 0 \\ w_j^* &= -fracG_jH_j + lambda endaligned
Step 5: score a tree, then a split. Put w_j^* back into the leaf's parabola to see how low it gets:

beginaligned &G_j w_j^* + tfrac12 (H_j + lambda)\, w_j^*^2 \\ &quad = -fracG_j^2H_j + lambda + fracG_j^22(H_j + lambda) \\ &quad = -fracG_j^22(H_j + lambda) \\ &Obj^* = -frac12 sum_j=1^T fracG_j^2H_j + lambda + gamma T endaligned

Obj^* is the structure score of a tree shape: the best it can do, computed from sums alone, with nothing refitted (lower is better; tutorials call G^2/(H + lambda) a leaf's similarity score). A split turns one leaf into two, which adds one leaf and costs gamma . Its gain is the drop in the structure score:
beginaligned Gain &= frac12 Big[ fracG_L^2H_L + lambda + fracG_R^2H_R + lambda \\ &qquad - frac(G_L + G_R)^2H_L + H_R + lambda Big] - gamma endaligned

In words: (left score + right score − the score without splitting), halved, minus the price of a leaf. The tree takes the split with the largest gain; if none is above 0, the node stays a leaf (exact XGBoost applies gamma afterwards, by pruning; section 07). You've done every step by hand already. The only new pieces are lambda in the denominators and gamma at the end; with lambda = 0 and gamma = 0 it's exactly section 05. One implementation detail: XGBoost stores eta\, w^* in each leaf, so its dumped leaf values already include the learning rate.
The first tree on the six rows again, now with lambda = 1 and gamma = 0 . Everything XGBoost computes at the root:

The whole node from sums: per-row g and h (all rows at p = 0.5 ), each side's G and H , the leaf weights -G/(H + lambda) and the gain. lambda pulls both leaves toward 0, and the smaller one ( H = 0.5 ) harder.

The leaves are −0.5 and +0.667, down from −1 and +2. After 3 trees ( eta = 0.3 ) this gives p = 0.404 for late ≤ 1 and 0.633 for late ≥ 2, and XGBoost itself (exact method, lambda = 1 , min_child_weight = 0) returns the same probabilities. Its tree dump shows a Gain of 1.167 for the split, because XGBoost drops the ½, and a Cover of 1.5, 1.0 and 0.5: cover is H .
The weighted least-squares view
Complete the square in each row's term from step 2:
g\, w + tfrac12 h\, w^2 = tfrac12 h Big(w + fracghBig)^2 - fracg^22h

The last part doesn't depend on w . So each XGBoost tree is a weighted least-squares fit to the targets -g/h , with weights h : each row asks for its own Newton step, weighted by how sure that step is. For squared error that's the residuals with weight 1, section 02 again. This view explains why the approximate split finder weights its quantiles by h (section 09).
Classic gradient boosting vs XGBoost
Squared error on -g (e.g. y - p ), as if h = 1
Newton step -G/H , filled in after the tree is grown
-G/(H + lambda) , the formula that chose the splits
Learning rate, tree size, row subsampling
Those, plus lambda , gamma , alpha , minimum child weight, column subsampling
Learned default direction per split
Histograms, parallel inside a tree, GPU, distributed
For squared error with lambda = 0 the two are the same algorithm, because h = 1 everywhere. LightGBM and sklearn's HistGradientBoosting use the same second-order gain.

In an interview: “XGBoost minimizes the loss plus gamma per leaf plus tfrac12lambdasum w^2 . It expands the loss to second order around the current prediction, so each row contributes g w + tfrac12 h w^2 . Grouping by leaf gives G w + tfrac12 (H + lambda) w^2 , minimized at w^* = -G/(H + lambda) ; plugging back gives -tfrac12 G^2/(H + lambda) per leaf, and the gain is the children's scores minus the parent's, halved, minus gamma . Equivalently, each tree is a weighted least-squares fit to -g/h with weights h .”

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: Every penalty answers the same failure: a leaf that takes a big step on little evidence. For log loss, “little evidence” has two forms: few rows, or rows the model is already sure about, whose h = p(1 - p) is tiny. Both make H small, and -G/H huge.

What each regularizer does, and why it exists
What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: Think of lambda as lambda units of hessian saying “don't move”, added to every leaf. It matters only where the real H is comparable to it: small leaves and confident regions. It also enters the gain, where it shrinks each child's score G^2/(H + lambda) , so splits that isolate a small group earn less. On the six rows, lambda = 1 holds the pure late 2–3 group's score to 3.9 after 200 trees, against 17.6 with lambda = 0 .

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: γ: a price per leaf, and pruning

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: A split must earn more than gamma , or it isn't worth the extra leaf. Two details matter at node level:

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: Units. XGBoost's code and dumps use the gain without the ½, and compare that number with gamma. The toy split's dumped gain is 1.167, so it survives gamma = 1.1 and is pruned at gamma = 1.2.

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: When it's applied. XGBoost's exact method grows the tree to max_depth first, then prunes bottom-up: a split is removed if its gain is below gamma and both its children are leaves. So a weak split with a strong split below it survives, which matters for patterns like XOR, where the first cut gains almost nothing but enables a big second one. With the default histogram method, gamma is checked as the tree grows instead, so a weak first cut is never made and an XOR-like pair can be missed.

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: gamma also caps the tree's size indirectly: on noisy data most deep splits have small gains, and a gamma on that scale removes them.

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: min_child_weight: a minimum hessian, not a row count

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: Each child needs H ge min_child_weight, or the split is refused. For squared error ( h = 1 ) that's a minimum row count. For log loss it counts rows weighted by how unsure the model is. Take 10 rows the model is 99% sure won't default ( p = 0.01 , h = 0.0099 each), one of which defaults anyway:

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: beginaligned G &= 10 times 0.01 - 1 \\ &= -0.9 \\ H &= 10 times 0.0099 \\ &= 0.099 \\ w_lambda = 0 &= 0.9 / 0.099 \\ &approx 9.1 \\ w_lambda = 1 &= 0.9 / 1.099 \\ &approx 0.82 endaligned

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: With lambda = 0 , one surprise would take the whole leaf from 1% risk to about 99% (before the learning rate). With the default min_child_weight = 1, the leaf isn't allowed at all, since H = 0.099 < 1 . At p = 0.03 ( h approx 0.029 ), it takes about 35 rows to reach H = 1 . So min_child_weight blocks leaves made of rows the model already has right, where a big step would only chase noise. Two consequences:

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: It tightens on its own as training goes on. As predictions grow confident, each row's h shrinks, so the same rows carry less weight and fewer splits pass.

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: The toy can't split at all under the default: every cut leaves one side with H below 1 (0.75, 0.5 or 0.25). Section 15 shows what that does.

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: alpha (L1) adds alpha sum_j lvert w_j rvert . The parabola gets a kink at 0, and the solution moves G toward 0 by alpha before dividing:

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: beginaligned w^* &= -fracsign(G)\, max(lvert G rvert - alpha,\ 0)H + lambda \\ leaf score &= fracmax(lvert G rvert - alpha,\ 0)^2H + lambda endaligned

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: A leaf whose lvert G rvert le alpha gets exactly 0, and the gain uses the thresholded G too. max_delta_step caps lvert w rvert directly; XGBoost suggests it for logistic loss on extremely imbalanced data, where H can be tiny. The learning rate, row subsampling and column subsampling regularize the ensemble rather than a leaf (sections 03 and 09).

chunks.h: What each regularizer does, and why it exists
chunks.x: In an interview: “ lambda adds to the hessian in every leaf, so it shrinks leaves with little hessian (few rows, or confident ones) and barely touches big leaves. gamma is the minimum gain for a split, a price per leaf: the exact method prunes bottom-up after growing, the histogram method refuses weak splits as it grows. min_child_weight is the minimum hessian sum per child; for log loss it blocks leaves made of rows the model is already sure about. alpha soft-thresholds G , so weak leaves go to exactly 0.”

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Real data has holes: a blank field, no credit history yet. XGBoost doesn't need them filled in. Its sparsity-aware split finding learns, at every split, which side the missing rows should go.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Scan only the rows where the feature is present, with running sums as usual.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Add up the missing rows' G_miss and H_miss once.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: At each cut, compute the gain twice: once with the missing rows added to the left side, once to the right.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Keep the better of all of these. The winning side is stored with the split as its default direction.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: At prediction time, a missing value follows its split's default direction.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Example. Add two applicants with no record of late payments, both of whom defaulted. Everyone is at p = 0.5 , and lambda = 1 :

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: So G_miss = -1 and H_miss = 0.5 .

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: One cut, scored twice. The present rows give left G = 1 , H = 1 and right G = -1 , H = 0.5 ; the missing rows add G = -1 , H = 0.5 to one side (shaded). The parent is G = -1 , H = 2 (score 1/3 with lambda = 1 ) either way. The higher gain wins and fixes the default direction.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: So missing values go right, with the risky “2+ late payments” group, which makes sense: both missing rows defaulted. XGBoost picks the same split, and its dump's Missing column points to the right child.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Missingness can carry signal. Here “no record” behaved like “risky”. Imputing the mean would have thrown that away; if you do impute (for a linear model, say), add a missing-indicator column.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: No missing values in training means no learned direction. Every split then has a fixed default side, which depends on the library, version and tree method. On the six rows, an applicant whose late count is missing gets, after section 05's two trees, 0.374 from this note's NumPy build (which breaks the tie to the left, the low-risk side) but 0.744 from XGBoost's default histogram method (which sends unseen missing values right). Either way it's a default nobody learned. In a simulated loan book, blanking one key feature for every test applicant sent them all to its high-risk side and dropped AU

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Sparse matrices: in XGBoost, entries that aren't stored count as missing, so if your zeros are real zeros, a sparse matrix silently turns them into “missing”. (LightGBM keeps unstored entries as zeros unless zero_as_missing=True.)

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Cost: the scan touches only present values, so very sparse features (one-hot columns, rare flags) are cheap.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: Other libraries: LightGBM and sklearn's HistGB also learn a side per split (HistGB sends unseen-in-training missing values to the child with more rows). CatBoost doesn't learn one: by default a missing value is treated as smaller than every real value, so it always goes to the low side.

chunks.h: Missing values: the learned default direction
chunks.x: In an interview: “At each split XGBoost scans only the present values, then tries adding the missing rows' G and H to the left and to the right, and keeps whichever gives the higher gain as that split's default direction. No imputation, missingness can carry signal, and it's cheap on sparse data. The risk: if a feature had no missing values in training, the direction is a fixed default, so values that go missing only in production all go one arbitrary way.”
Exact greedy: running sums

Sort the rows by a feature, then sweep left to right, adding each row's g and h to G_L and H_L , with G_R = G - G_L and H_R = H - H_L . Every cut between distinct values is scored in one pass, with nothing refitted: that's why the gain needs only sums. XGBoost sorts each feature once before training (it stores the data in sorted column blocks), so each node costs one linear sweep per feature over its rows. Exact, but every distinct value is a candidate, which is slow on millions of rows.
Approximate: quantiles weighted by h

Instead of every value, propose candidate cuts at quantiles of the feature, with each row weighted by its hessian h_i , so every bucket holds about the same total h . Why h : by the weighted least-squares view (section 06), each row is a squared-error target with weight h , so rows the model is unsure about ( p near 0.5) count more and get finer cut points, while confident rows get coarse ones. The candidates can be proposed once per tree (global) or again at every node (local). A weighted quantile sketch is a small summary that answers these weighted quantile questions within a set error and
Histograms: the modern default
Once, before training, cut each feature into at most about 256 bins at its quantiles, and store each row's bin number (one byte).
At each node, add up g and h per bin: one pass over the node's rows.
Sweep the bin edges with running sums, scoring at most 255 candidates.
Sibling subtraction: a parent's histogram is the sum of its children's, so build the smaller child's histogram and get the bigger one's by subtraction. That at least halves the work at every level.
Where the speed comes from: far fewer candidates; one-byte codes, so passes over the rows are small and cache-friendly; histograms add up across threads, machines and GPUs.

The price: a cut can only land on a bin edge. In a simulated book, the best income threshold moved from 39.46 to 39.66 and lost 0.6% of its gain with 255 bins; with only 8 bins it moved to 48.6 and lost about a quarter. Quantile bins also shrug off outliers, which just share the last bin.
XGBoost (tree_method="hist", the default), LightGBM, CatBoost and sklearn's HistGradientBoosting all work this way.
Column subsampling, and parallelism

Column subsampling lets each tree (colsample_bytree), each level (bylevel) or each split (bynode) see a random share of the features; the three multiply, so 0.5 each on 64 features leaves 8 per split. It decorrelates the trees as in a random forest, speeds things up, and stops one dominant feature from taking every split, at the risk of missing the best feature at some nodes.

Parallel, but not across trees. Each tree needs the previous one's F , so trees are built in sequence. The parallelism is inside a tree: g and h for all rows, histogram building, and the scans over different features all run at once.

In an interview: “Exact search sorts each feature once and sweeps every distinct value with running sums of g and h . The approximate method proposes candidates at quantiles weighted by h , because each row is a squared-error target with weight h . Histogram search bins each feature once into about 256 quantile bins, sums g and h per bin in one pass, scans only bin edges, and gets one child's histogram free by subtraction. The price is a little threshold precision.”

LightGBM uses the same core: g , h , the leaf score G^2/(H + lambda) , the same gain (reported without the ½) and leaves -G/(H + lambda) , with histograms by design. What differs is how a tree grows, plus two speed tricks and native categories. Its defaults also differ: lambda = 0 , 31 leaves, at least 20 rows per leaf, learning rate 0.1.
Depth-wise vs leaf-wise growth
Four leaves, three ways. Circles are splits, squares are leaves. Leaf-wise spends every split where the gain is largest, so one branch can run deep; symmetric asks one question per level (A, then B).
Depth-wise (level-wise) splits every leaf at the current depth, then goes one level deeper. XGBoost's default (grow_policy="depthwise"); a depth- d tree has up to 2^d leaves.
Leaf-wise (best-first) splits, of all current leaves, the one whose best split gains most, until there are num_leaves leaves. LightGBM's way; XGBoost does it with grow_policy="lossguide".
Why leaf-wise: for the same number of leaves it usually lowers the training loss more, because it never spends a split on a leaf with little to gain.

The risk: deep, thin branches that fit a handful of rows. On a simulated loan book, LightGBM's first 8-leaf tree went one level deeper than a depth-3 tree could, isolating a 20-row group, and spent a split on a decoy feature.
num_leaves is the main capacity knob. Validation log loss on the simulated book, learning rate 0.05, 500 rounds:

More leaves reach their best sooner, then overfit much faster. On small data min_child_samples (a row count, unlike XGBoost's hessian sum) is what stops it: with 400 training rows, allowing one-row leaves gave a best loss of 0.272, against 0.237 with 50-row leaves. max_depth is an extra cap; if it's set, 2^depth bounds the leaves, so use one main knob and keep the other loose.
GOSS: sample the rows that still teach something

Gradient-based one-side sampling. Rows with small lvert g rvert are already well fitted and add little to any split's gain. So keep the top a share of rows by lvert g rvert (say 20%; the paper ranks by lvert g rvert , LightGBM's code by lvert g h rvert , and it skips sampling for the first 1/eta rounds), sample b of all rows (say 10%) from the rest, and give each sampled row the weight (1 - a)/b = 8 , since it stands in for 8 rows. The reweighting keeps G and H unbiased: without it the sums would come from the hardest rows only, and the leaves would overshoot toward them. Each tree sees 30% of
EFB: bundle features that are never on together

Exclusive feature bundling. Sparse features that are rarely non-zero at the same time (one-hot columns, say) are merged into one feature, with each original's values shifted into its own range of bins, so a split can still separate them. Fewer histograms to build. Finding the best bundling is a graph-colouring problem, so it's done greedily, allowing a small rate of conflicts. Neither GOSS nor EFB defines LightGBM; its core is histograms plus leaf-wise growth.
Native categorical splits

Give LightGBM a column of category codes and it finds a good way to split the categories into two groups without trying all 2^k-1 groupings: it sorts the categories by G/(H + s) , a Newton-style value per category with s = cat_smooth, and scans that order like a numeric feature. With plain G/H , for squared error and the lambda = 0 gain, the best two-group split is always a cut of that sorted order (Fisher, 1958); with the smoothing it's a good heuristic rather than a guarantee. Very few categories (up to 4 by default) get one-vs-rest splits instead.

cat_smooth (default 10) does two jobs: categories with fewer rows than it are left out of the sorted scan (they go to the “other” side), and it adds pseudo-hessian to the rest, so a small category can't reach an extreme of the order by luck.
Other guards: cat_l2 adds to lambda for these splits, max_cat_threshold limits how many categories the scan can put on one side, and min_data_per_group sets a minimum per side.
The risk: with hundreds of rare levels it can still overfit. On a useless 300-level pincode it dropped test AUC from 0.811 to 0.753, until cat_smooth was raised to 100.

XGBoost does the same with the histogram method and enable_categorical=True: a feature with at most max_cat_to_onehot levels gets one-vs-rest splits; otherwise its categories are sorted by their leaf weight -G/(H + lambda) and the order is scanned like a number, with at most max_cat_threshold categories on one side. Same idea, same small-category risk.

In an interview: “LightGBM is histogram-based and grows leaf-wise: it always splits the leaf with the largest gain, so for the same number of leaves it lowers training loss faster, but it can grow deep, thin branches that overfit small data. num_leaves is the main capacity knob, with min_child_samples and max_depth as guards. GOSS keeps the large-gradient rows and an up-weighted sample of the rest; EFB bundles mutually exclusive sparse features. Categories are split by sorting them on G/H .”

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: The problem with categories

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: A categorical feature with many levels (pincode, merchant ID, branch) is awkward for trees. One-hot encoding makes hundreds of sparse, individually weak columns; integer codes impose an order that means nothing. Target encoding replaces each category by its average target (“pincode 110034 → 12% default rate”): compact and powerful. But computed on the same rows the model trains on, it leaks: each row's own label is inside its category's average.

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: How big the leak is. In a simulated loan book, give every applicant a random pincode, 300 of them, with no effect on default. A pincode has about 12 training rows, so when one of them defaults, its own label lifts its pincode's rate by about 1/12, or 8 points. On training rows the encoding “knows” the answer; on test rows it's noise.

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: Train AUC of the column alone

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: Test AUC of the column alone

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: The model trusted a strong signal that wasn't there. Smoothing toward the prior doesn't fix it: it pulls every encoding toward the mean but keeps their order almost exactly when categories have similar counts (here about 12 rows each), and splits and AUC only use the order (train AUC stayed at 0.78). The extreme case is an ID-like column with a new value for every row: naive encoding hands each row its own label, a train AUC of 1.0.

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: Ordered target statistics

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: Put the training rows in a random order and encode each row using only the rows before it with the same category, as if the data arrived one row at a time. A row's own label never enters its own encoding:

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: hat x_i = fracsum_j prec i,\ c_j = c_i y_j + a cdot prior\#\\, j prec i : c_j = c_i \,\ + a

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: In words: j prec i means “before row i in the random order”. The prior (the overall rate) counts as a extra rows, so the first rows of a category, which have seen almost nothing, get an encoding near the prior instead of a wild value. Test rows use all the training rows. The early rows of each permutation get noisy encodings, so CatBoost uses several random permutations. An unseen category at inference gets the prior. With a real time order, has_time=True uses it instead of a random one, which matches how data arrives in production.

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: Ordered boosting: the prediction-shift problem

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: The same leak happens inside boosting itself. Row i 's gradient g_i is computed from a model that was trained on row i , so on training rows the residuals are systematically smaller than they would be on new rows: the model's training predictions are shifted toward their own labels. The trees are then fitted to gradients that look better than reality, which is a bias, worst on small data. Ordered boosting computes each row's gradient from a model built only on the rows before it in the permutation, so no row's gradient comes from a model that saw it. Keeping one model per prefix would be far t

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: Symmetric (oblivious) trees

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: Every node at the same depth asks the same question (the figure in section 10). A depth-6 tree is just 6 (feature, threshold) pairs and 64 leaves, and a row's leaf index is its 6 yes/no answers read as a 6-bit number. Prediction is a few comparisons and one array lookup, with no branching, so it vectorizes well and is very fast. Each level's question is chosen by its total improvement across every node of the level. The rigid shape is also a strong regularizer: 6 splits instead of up to 63, and no branch can carve out a handful of rows on its own. The cost is flexibility per tree, so it may ne

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: CatBoost also builds combinations of categorical features (pincode × product) greedily as trees grow, with their own ordered statistics, and its defaults are strong: untuned, it scored 0.827 / 0.221 (AUC / log loss) on the simulated book where sklearn's untuned HistGB scored 0.808 / 0.250. Missing values aren't learned: by default they're treated as the smallest value.

chunks.h: CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
chunks.x: In an interview: “Naive target encoding leaks, because each row's own label is inside its category's average, so a useless high-cardinality feature looks predictive on training rows and hurts on test. CatBoost's ordered target statistics encode each row using only the rows before it in a random permutation, plus a prior. Ordered boosting applies the same idea to the gradients, fixing prediction shift. Its symmetric trees ask one question per level, so the leaf index is a bit string: very fast inference and strong regularization.”
Fewer trees needed; noisier fit, worse best score
Bias down; variance up past the best round
Higher-order interactions; bias down, variance up
(Lowering them) variance down, a little bias up
reg_lambda, reg_alpha, gamma

Depth sets the interaction order. A stump uses one feature, so a sum of stumps is a sum of one-feature effects, f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + dots , and can't make a jump that happens only when A and B are true. For a 0/1 target that's 1 only when both are 1 (the four combinations equally common), the best a sum of stumps can do in squared error is −0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.75; a depth-2 tree gets 0, 0, 0, 1 exactly. On a smooth simulated target, stumps scored an RMSE of 20.5 (no better than linear regression) and depth 2 scored 10.5.
A tuning order that works
Fix eta at 0.05–0.1, set the number of trees high, and early-stop. Never grid-search the number of trees: one fit with early stopping reads the best round off the validation curve.
Tree size with leaf size: max_depth or num_leaves, together with min_child_weight or min_child_samples. These usually matter most.
Randomness: subsample and colsample_bytree.
Penalties: lambda , alpha , gamma .
Lower eta (to 0.01–0.02), early-stop again, and refit.
Score once on the test set.

Why this order: eta and the tree count trade off almost one for one, so fixing eta removes a redundant dimension; capacity has the biggest effect; randomness and penalties fine-tune what's left; and a smaller eta at the end buys a slightly better minimum for more trees. Put eta into a random search and the search drifts to tiny rates and slow models, because a smaller rate with more trees almost always looks a little better. Random search or Bayesian optimization beats a grid for steps 2–4. On the simulated book, this took validation log loss from 0.234 (defaults) to 0.226, and the winner was
Early stopping, done right

Keep the best round after a patience of, say, 50 rounds. LightGBM and XGBoost's sklearn API predict with the best round (with native xgb.train, pass iteration_range=(0, bst.best_iteration + 1)); sklearn's HistGB keeps the trees it built while waiting, so keep its patience small or refit.

The validation set must look like production. For credit or anything time-dependent, validate on a later period (out-of-time), with each customer on one side only. A random split of a drifting book stops at the wrong round.

Never early-stop on the test set: the round is then chosen for those rows, and no honest estimate is left. On the simulated book, stopping on test picked 24 trees and reported 0.218; stopping on validation picked 15 trees, which scored 0.220 on test.
Stop on the metric you'll use. AUC only cares about order and can stop where probabilities are still off; stop on log loss when the probability itself is used (pricing, expected loss).

In an interview: “Fix the learning rate at 0.05–0.1 and let early stopping pick the number of trees. Then tune tree size with minimum leaf size, then subsampling, then the penalties, and finally lower the learning rate and early-stop again. Depth and leaves lower bias and raise variance; minimum child weight, subsampling and the penalties do the reverse. All of it on a validation set that mirrors deployment, out-of-time for credit, with the test set used once.”
Class imbalance and scale_pos_weight

scale_pos_weight = k multiplies every positive row's g and h by k , exactly as if each positive appeared k times. The model then fits the reweighted data, whose odds are k times the real ones. For one group, the weighted best constant solves
beginaligned k\, n_+ (p - 1) + n_-\, p &= 0 \\ fracp1 - p &= k\, fracn_+n_- endaligned
In words: the zero-slope condition of the weighted log loss, with n_+ positives and n_- negatives; the predicted odds come out at k times the true odds n_+/n_- .
On the six rows, k = 2 (still starting at p = 0.5 ): the root gain rises from 0.583 to 0.709, and the leaves become −0.222 and +1.0 (from −0.5 and +0.667): positives pull harder everywhere.

At k = 50 : an applicant with a true 3% risk has odds 0.031; times 50 that's 1.55, so a well-fitted model says about 0.61. In a simulated book with 8.7% defaults, a 100-tree depth-3 XGBoost model's mean prediction became 0.55, and its AUC fell from 0.825 to 0.794.
Fix the probabilities by subtracting log k from the raw score, or by recalibrating on held-out data.

Do you need it at all? Often not. Starting at the log-odds of the base rate already balances the gradients ( sum g = 0 at the start), and log loss is fine with rare positives. If you only need a ranking or a decision, keep the plain loss and move the threshold. Weighting can help when positives are so rare that splits on them can't clear min_child_weight; max_delta_step is the other knob for that case.

Credit models are expected to move one way in some features: predicted risk mustn't fall as late payments rise, or rise as income rises. An unconstrained booster fits some noise, so in places a richer applicant gets a higher risk, which is hard to defend to a customer or a regulator and is usually overfitting anyway. A monotonic constraint forces the prediction to move only one way in a feature, with every other feature held fixed. It's enforced while the tree grows:

Reject violating splits. For a split on a feature constrained to increase, a candidate whose left (lower-value) child gets a larger weight than its right child is refused (its gain is treated as -infty ).

Pass bounds down. After an accepted split with child weights w_L le w_R , the midpoint m = (w_L + w_R)/2 becomes an upper bound for every leaf in the left subtree and a lower bound for every leaf in the right subtree. Later splits, on any feature, inherit these bounds.
Clip leaf values into their bounds, so nothing deeper down can undo the order.
Each tree is then monotone in that feature, and a sum of monotone functions is monotone, so the whole model is.

On a simulated loan book, unconstrained XGBoost's average risk curve rose with income at 12 of 27 steps, and every applicant's own curve rose somewhere. Constrained (income −1, EMI share and late payments +1), no curve rose anywhere, test log loss was unchanged (0.222 → 0.221), and AUC fell from 0.832 to 0.811; on a test set this size a gap like that is partly luck (the true probabilities themselves score 0.817). A wrong constraint shows up as a flat curve and a worse score: forcing risk to rise with income took log loss to 0.262.

Caveats: the constraint holds with other features fixed, which can differ from the raw trend (if higher earners take bigger loans, raw default rates can rise with income even though, at a fixed loan size, they fall); and it says nothing about where missing values go, which is the learned default direction. LightGBM offers three enforcement methods (monotone_constraints_method): “basic” is the midpoint bounding above, the most restrictive; “intermediate” and “advanced” compute tighter, less restrictive bounds. Interaction constraints are the sibling tool: they say which features may share a tre
Feature importance: gain, split count, cover, SHAP
How many splits use the feature
Continuous, many-valued features, including noise ones
Average gain of those splits
Features used in one big early split per tree
Closer to SHAP, still training-data based
Average H reaching those splits (rows, for squared error)
Average size of each feature's contribution to predictions
Consistent; still describes the model, not the world

On a simulated book with a useless age feature, the shares were: weight 0.29 for age (split often, because it has many thresholds) and 0.05 for late payments (6 values, one big split per tree); gain 0.65 for late payments; mean |SHAP| put income and late payments on top and still gave age 0.11. All three built-in types are computed on training data, so they reward noise splits, and gain-based importance isn't consistent: a model can come to rely more on a feature while its gain importance falls. Prefer mean |SHAP|, or permutation importance on held-out data. With near-duplicate features, boost
TreeSHAP in one paragraph

A SHAP value splits one prediction into per-feature contributions that add up exactly to the raw score: F(x) = phi_0 + sum_j phi_j , with phi_0 the average score, in log-odds for a classifier. Each phi_j is a Shapley value: feature j 's extra contribution when it “joins”, averaged over every order in which features could join, where a feature that hasn't joined is averaged out. For a rule “risk = 1 if income < 40k AND EMI share > 0.5”, with those conditions true for 19% and 38% of applicants independently (base 0.072), a flagged applicant gets 0.56 for income and 0.37 for EMI: the rarer condit
Custom objectives, ranking, offsets and DART

Custom objectives: XGBoost and LightGBM accept a function that returns g and h for every row; that's all the tree builder needs. h must stay positive (libraries clip it to a small floor), so a loss with zero or negative curvature breaks -G/(H + lambda) and the gain. The evaluation metric is separate from the objective.

Ranking (LambdaMART): within each query, every pair of items gets a “lambda” gradient weighted by how much swapping them would change NDCG; each item's lambdas sum to its g (with a matching h ), and trees are grown as usual. Keep each query's rows together when splitting the data.

Offsets and continued training: base_margin (XGBoost) or init_score (LightGBM) gives each row its own starting score instead of one F_0 , such as log exposure in a Poisson model or an earlier model's score; boosting continues from it. Passing an existing model (xgb_model) adds trees to it.
DART drops a random few of the existing trees when computing each round's gradients, so no early tree dominates. It regularizes, but it's slower and doesn't combine well with early stopping.
Why boosting overfits noisy labels more than a random forest

Boosting puts each new tree where the remaining error is, and a mislabelled or unpredictable row stays in the remaining error. On the six rows, row 3 (a defaulter that looks like the non-defaulters) has g = −0.5 at the start, −0.574 after one tree, −0.70 after ten, and settles at −0.667, while row 5's g falls to −0.002. The unfixable row ends up with one of the largest gradients in the data, round after round, and deeper trees will spend splits isolating it. A random forest fits each tree to the labels with every row weighted equally; a noisy row distorts a few leaves in some trees, and averag

Every tree is flat beyond its last split, so the sum is too. An applicant with 10 late payments gets the same 66.35 as one with 3. In a simulated book, a booster predicted a credit limit of 242.6 at incomes of 150, 300 and 600 (₹k), where the truth was 240, 480 and 960. Fixes: predict a quantity that stays in range (limit ÷ income), detrend first and boost the residual of a linear model, or use linear leaves (LightGBM's linear_tree).

A booster trained on log loss and early-stopped on log loss is often reasonably calibrated, because log loss rewards honest probabilities. It drifts when: you go past the best round (on the six rows, 200 trees took one- and two-row groups to 0.000 and 1.000); you use scale_pos_weight, class weights or undersampling (odds × k ); you use a large eta or tiny leaves. Check a reliability curve on held-out, out-of-time data, and fix it with Platt scaling (a logistic regression on the raw score, good with little data) or isotonic regression (more flexible, needs more data), fitted on data not used fo

In an interview: “scale_pos_weight multiplies the positives' g and h , so the model learns k times the odds: subtract log k or recalibrate, or just move the threshold. Monotone constraints are enforced at split time: violating splits are rejected and midpoint bounds pass down to the leaves, so every tree, and the sum, is monotone. Split-count and gain importances are biased and computed on training data; use SHAP or permutation importance. Boosting chases unfixable rows, can't extrapolate, and needs a calibration check after any reweighting.”

chunks.h: Boosting vs random forest vs neural nets on tables
chunks.x: Where the forest sits: a random forest shares the trees' column (no preprocessing, robust to useless features, flat outside the range, TreeSHAP). It differs from boosting as in section 01: it cuts variance rather than bias, doesn't overfit with more trees, needs little tuning and trains in parallel, and usually scores a little lower once both are tuned. It's the safer choice when you can't validate carefully.

chunks.h: Boosting vs random forest vs neural nets on tables
chunks.x: Why trees win on most tables. Benchmarks on medium-sized tabular data (Grinsztajn et al., 2022) point to three reasons. Real tabular targets are irregular, full of thresholds and steps, and neural nets are biased toward smooth functions. Useless columns hurt an MLP much more than a tree, which simply never splits on them. And each column has its own meaning: trees work feature by feature, while an MLP treats the inputs as a rotatable vector and has to learn which directions matter.

chunks.h: Boosting vs random forest vs neural nets on tables
chunks.x: When neural nets win: very large data; raw images, text or audio inside the row; sequences such as transaction histories; many tasks sharing learned embeddings; end-to-end training with other modalities. Tabular foundation models trained to do in-context learning are now competitive on small tables. Ensembles of a booster and a neural net often beat either alone.

Every tree goes in at full size, noise and all. On the six rows, one tree takes the late 2–3 group from 0.5 to 0.88, on two rows, and two trees to 0.96. For log loss a full Newton step from far away also overshoots, because the parabola is only accurate near the current point: in a simulated book, one full step took a group with a real 30.5% default rate from the 8.7% base rate to 58%. Validation loss bottoms early and high ( eta = 0.5 was best after 2 trees at 0.239, against 0.232 for small rates) and then climbs fast. Given the same residuals, eta doesn't change which split wins; but a full
…the trees are very deep?

Each tree fits the current residuals almost exactly, noise included. With full-depth trees and eta = 0.1 , every round leaves 90% of each residual and the next tree refits the same pattern, so after 200 rounds the sum is about 1 - 0.9^200 approx 1 times one memorizing tree: a test RMSE of 13.5 in a simulated book, no better than a single deep tree (13.9), against 10.3 for depth-3 trees. Boosting reduces bias; a deep tree has no bias left to reduce, only variance, and adding deep trees in sequence doesn't average it away. Depth also raises the interaction order and shrinks leaves, so min_child_

Leaves become -G/H , so a leaf with a tiny hessian sum takes a huge step: 10 confident rows with one surprise default give 9.1 in log-odds instead of 0.82. Pure groups climb without limit: on the six rows the late 2–3 score reaches 17.6 after 200 trees, against 3.9 with lambda = 1 . With squared error and big leaves, lambda = 0 barely matters, since H is a row count. LightGBM's default is lambda = 0 , relying on min_child_samples instead.
…there's no early stopping?

Training loss keeps falling; validation loss is a U and climbs past the best round. In a simulated book at eta = 0.1 , the best was 15 trees (0.232), and 600 trees reached 0.301 while training loss fell to 0.044. Probabilities grow overconfident: on the six rows, 200 trees push the late 1 and late 2–3 groups to 0.000 and 1.000. A small eta makes the climb slower, not absent.
…min_child_weight is huge?

No split can give both children enough hessian, so every tree is a single leaf, w = -G/(H + lambda) : a constant shift. At the base-rate start G = 0 , so the model never moves from F_0 . On the six rows even the default of 1 does this (every cut leaves a side with H < 1 ): five trees, all single leaves of value 0, and every applicant stays at 0.5. Less extreme values bite harder as training goes on, because confident rows carry less hessian. High bias, by design.
…a feature is duplicated?

With exact search, the copy offers exactly the same gains, so ties are broken by a fixed rule and predictions don't change. Two things do change: with column subsampling, the duplicated feature is twice as likely to be offered at each tree or node, so it's effectively up-weighted; and importances. Without column subsampling every tie goes to the same copy (XGBoost prefers the lower column index), so one copy takes all the splits and the other shows zero; with column subsampling each copy wins when the other isn't offered, so the credit is split between them. Near-duplicates with a little noise
…one label is a big outlier?

For regression with squared error, that row's residual is huge and dominates G in every leaf it lands in, so every tree bends toward it; in a simulated book, a 2% share of +₹500k typos took test RMSE from about 10 to 29.0, while absolute error (10.5) and Huber (10.9) shrugged it off. For classification a flipped label caps at lvert g rvert le 1 but never goes away (section 13), so deeper trees isolate it. Use a robust loss, early stopping and bigger leaves, and look at the rows with the largest final gradients: they're often label errors.
…every feature is missing for a row?

The row follows the default direction at every split, so in each tree it lands in one fixed leaf: the end of the “all-missing” path. Its prediction is F_0 plus eta times those leaves, which isn't the base rate and isn't a considered estimate either. Each default direction was learned from rows where that one feature was missing (or not learned at all), not from rows where everything was. On the six rows, after two trees, a missing late count gets 0.374 (the low-risk value) from this note's NumPy build and 0.744 (the high-risk value) from XGBoost's default histogram method: two arbitrary defaul
…you start from 0 instead of the base rate? The first trees spend themselves walking everyone to the base rate; the end point is the same, the early rounds are wasted.
…you fit the gradient instead of the negative gradient? Every step goes uphill and training loss rises each round. It's the classic from-scratch bug; the check is that training loss falls.

…the trees are fitted in parallel on the same target? They come out nearly the same, so the sum is one tree with a bigger step. The correction only happens because tree m sees what trees 1 to m - 1 got wrong.

…the base learner is linear? A sum of linear models is one linear model, so boosting adds nothing a regularized linear fit doesn't have. Trees work because sums of steps build curves and interactions.
…a category at inference was never seen? CatBoost gives it the prior; LightGBM sends it down the “other” side of each categorical split; one-hot gives all zeros.
Generic gradient boosting (any loss)

INPUT X, y, loss, M trees, eta F0 = argmin_c Σ_i loss(y_i, c) # mean | median | log-odds of rate F[i] = F0 for every row i repeat M times: r[i] = -∂loss(y_i, F[i]) / ∂F[i] # pseudo-residuals tree = regression tree on (X, r), by squared error # picks the regions for each leaf j: c[j] = argmin_c Σ_(i in j) loss(y_i, F[i] + c) # mean / median / Newton F[i] += eta * c[leaf of row i] save (tree, c) PREDICT(x): s = F0 + eta * Σ_m c_m[leaf_m(x)] regression: return s classification: return sigmoid(s)
XGBoost: one round and one tree

each round: for every row i: g[i], h[i] = slope, bend at F[i] # squared: g = F - y, h = 1 # log loss: p = sigmoid(F) # g = p - y, h = p * (1 - p) tree = GROW(all rows, depth = 0) F[i] += eta * tree(x_i) GROW(rows, depth): G = Σ g; H = Σ h # over these rows if depth == max_depth: return LEAF(-G / (H + lam)) best = SPLIT_SEARCH(rows, G, H) if best.gain <= 0: return LEAF(-G / (H + lam)) split rows by best.f < best.cut # missing f → best.default side return NODE(best, GROW(left, depth + 1), GROW(right, depth + 1))
One split search, with the default direction

SPLIT_SEARCH(rows, G, H): best.gain = -infinity for each feature f: M = rows where f is missing Gm = Σ g over M; Hm = Σ h over M P = rows with f present, sorted by f GL = 0; HL = 0 for k = 0 .. len(P) - 2: GL += g[P[k]]; HL += h[P[k]] if f(P[k]) == f(P[k+1]): continue # no cut inside ties for side in (left, right): gl, hl = GL, HL if side == left: gl += Gm; hl += Hm gr = G - gl; hr = H - hl if min(hl, hr) < min_child_weight: continue gain = 1/2 * ( gl²/(hl + lam) + gr²/(hr + lam) - G²/(H + lam) ) - gamma if gain > best.gain: cut = (f(P[k]) + f(P[k+1])) / 2 best = (gain, f, cut, side) return be

Cost: sorting once per feature before training makes each node one linear sweep per feature; histograms replace the sorted rows by at most 256 bins. With gamma , XGBoost's exact method then prunes bottom-up any split whose gain is below gamma and whose children are both leaves.
