Both lower confidence, by different routes, and neither is a calibration method on its own. Measure.

Cross-entropy is unforgiving of wrong labels. A mislabelled example gets a tiny p_t for its (wrong) label, so its loss -log p_t is huge and its gradient as large as any example's. A big network eventually memorizes it (deep networks can fit even random labels); clean patterns tend to be learned first, so early stopping helps. The robust alternatives limit how hard a low-confidence example can pull:

MAE on probabilities, 2(1 - p_t) , is symmetric: its sum over all K possible labels is a constant, which makes it provably robust to uniform label noise. The price is slow, under-fitting training: its gradient is the cross-entropy gradient times 2p_t , so hard examples barely move it.

Generalized cross-entropy interpolates between the two, with 0 < kappa le 1 . As kappa to 0 it becomes -log p_t ; at kappa = 1 it's 1 - p_t . Its gradient is the cross-entropy gradient times p_t^kappa , so low-confidence, possibly mislabelled examples are down-weighted.
L_kappa = frac1 - p_t^kappakappa

Bootstrapping blends the given label with the model's own prediction, beta y + (1 - beta)hat p (or with its argmax), so a confident model can partly overrule a wrong label. Label smoothing is the same blend with the uniform distribution instead of the model, which is why it also buys some robustness to noise.
Other common fixes: train only on the small-loss examples (co-teaching), or estimate the label-noise transition matrix and correct the loss with it.

A model is calibrated when P(y = 1 mid hat p = p) = p : of the cases it scores at 0.8, 80% are positive. A reliability diagram bins predictions by confidence and plots each bin's accuracy against its mean confidence; perfect calibration is the diagonal. The expected calibration error is the weighted average gap:
ECE = sum_b=1^M frac|B_b|N\,Big|acc(B_b) - conf(B_b)Big|

For multi-class it's usually computed on the top-1 confidence. It depends on the binning (equal-width or equal-count), is biased when bins are small, and can be gamed: always predicting the base rate is perfectly calibrated and useless. Report it next to log loss or the Brier score, which measure calibration and sharpness together.

Why modern networks are over-confident: once the training set is classified correctly, cross-entropy keeps falling by growing the logits. The validation NLL starts overfitting before the accuracy does. Depth, width, BatchNorm and less weight decay all made it worse (Guo et al., 2017).
Proper scoring rules (log loss, Brier) are minimized in expectation only by the true probability, so they reward honest probabilities. Accuracy, hinge and focal loss are not proper.
After training, freeze the network and fit one scalar T > 0 on held-out data by minimizing the NLL of the rescaled logits:
T^* = argmin_T \; -sum_i in val logsoftmaxbig(z_i / Tbig)_y_i
Every logit is divided by the same T , so the argmax, and hence accuracy, is unchanged. T > 1 softens an over-confident model.
One parameter can barely overfit the validation set, and it works remarkably well for neural networks.
Relatives: Platt scaling (binary, sigma(a z + b) ); vector and matrix scaling (per-class, more parameters); isotonic regression (non-parametric and monotone, needs more data, can create ties).
Calibration is fitted to one distribution; recheck it after any shift. And if the model was trained with weights or resampling, apply the prior correction first (or let the calibrator absorb it).
With labels y in \-1, +1\ , the margin m = y z is positive when the prediction is right and large when it's confidently right. Classification losses can be compared as functions of m alone.

The 0–1 loss (what accuracy counts) is a step: flat everywhere, so its gradient is useless. Hinge, logistic and exponential losses are convex upper bounds on it, with useful slopes. The logistic loss is a bound in base 2, as drawn; with natural logs it bounds the step up to a factor 1/log 2 . Hinge reaches exactly zero at margin 1; the logistic loss never does.
zero beyond the margin; no probabilities
differentiable; punishes violations more
never exactly zero; gives probabilities
AdaBoost's loss; explodes on mislabelled points

Once a point is beyond the margin ( m ge 1 ) its loss and gradient are exactly zero, so it stops influencing the model. The SVM solution depends only on the points on or inside the margin, the support vectors. The logistic loss keeps pushing every point a little.
Its population minimizer is sign(2p - 1) : it estimates the best decision, not the probability. That's why SVM scores aren't probabilities and need Platt scaling.
Hinge plus lambdalVert wrVert^2 is the soft-margin SVM; the margin width is 2/lVert wrVert .
Multi-class version (Weston–Watkins): the true class must beat every other class by a margin Delta :
L = sum_j ne c maxbig(0,\ Delta + z_j - z_cbig)
Ranking: pointwise, pairwise, listwise

Ranking is usually judged by NDCG: a gain for each item, discounted by the log of its rank and normalized by the best possible ordering's score (IDCG), so it lies in [0, 1] . With rel_i the relevance of the item at rank i :
beginaligned DCG@k &= sum_i=1^k frac2^rel_i - 1log_2(1 + i) \\ NDCG@k &= fracDCG@kIDCG@k endaligned
Pointwise: predict each item's relevance on its own, with MSE or BCE. Simple, but it ignores that only the order within a query matters.
Pairwise (RankNet): for a pair where item i should rank above j , model P(i succ j) = sigma(s_i - s_j) and train with BCE:
beginaligned L_ij &= logBig(1 + e^-(s_i - s_j)Big) \\ fracpartial L_ijpartial s_i &= -\,sigmabig(-(s_i - s_j)big) \\ fracpartial L_ijpartial s_j &= +\,sigmabig(-(s_i - s_j)big) endaligned

The same loss with a sampled negative item is BPR (Bayesian personalized ranking), the standard implicit-feedback recommender loss. Its weakness: a mis-ordered pair costs the same at rank 50 as at rank 1, but users only look at the top.

Reward models and DPO use the same pairwise logistic loss. An RLHF reward model uses the Bradley–Terry model, P(y_w succ y_l mid x) = sigmabig(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)big) for a preferred response y_w and a rejected one y_l , and minimizes -logsigma(r_w - r_l) : RankNet on (chosen, rejected) pairs. Direct preference optimization (DPO) drops the reward model and uses the policy's log-ratio to a frozen reference model as an implicit reward:
beginaligned hat r(x, y) &= betalogfracpi_theta(y mid x)pi_ref(y mid x) \\ L_DPO &= -logsigmabig(hat r(x, y_w) - hat r(x, y_l)big) endaligned

Its gradient raises the chosen response's log-probability and lowers the rejected one's, weighted by sigma(hat r_l - hat r_w) : by how wrongly the implicit reward orders the pair now. beta plays the role of the KL penalty's strength; a smaller beta lets the policy drift further from the reference.

LambdaRank skips writing a loss and defines the gradient directly: take RankNet's pair gradient and scale it by how much NDCG would change if the two items swapped places. A document's total gradient is the sum of its lambda s over all its pairs. Pairs near the top get large gradients; swaps deep in the list hardly count. LambdaMART is these gradients fed to gradient-boosted trees (lambdarank in LightGBM; rank:ndcg in XGBoost, which also has rank:pairwise and rank:map).
|lambda_ij| = sigmabig(-(s_i - s_j)big)\,big|DeltaNDCG_ijbig|

Listwise: score the whole list at once. ListNet uses cross-entropy between the softmax of the true relevances and the softmax of the scores; ListMLE maximizes the likelihood of the correct order under a Plackett–Luce model. Softmax cross-entropy over a list with one relevant item and sampled negatives is the sampled softmax, which is InfoNCE (next section). When negatives are sampled (in-batch, or by popularity) rather than drawn from the whole catalogue, frequently sampled items get pushed down too often and the softmax is biased against popular items. The logQ correction subtracts log Q(j) ,
NDCG itself depends on a sort, so it's piecewise constant in the scores and its gradient is zero almost everywhere. That's why all of the above exist.

The goal is an embedding f(x) where similar items are close and dissimilar ones far apart: retrieval, face verification, recommendation, self-supervised pretraining, CLIP. Embeddings are usually L2-normalized. Then the similarity of two embeddings e_1, e_2 is the cosine s = e_1^top e_2 in [-1, 1] , their squared distance is 2 - 2s , and the trivial win of scaling every embedding up is gone.
Contrastive (pairwise) loss
For a pair at distance d , labelled y = 1 (similar) or y = 0 (dissimilar), with margin m :

Positive pairs are always pulled together. Negative pairs are pushed apart only until they're m apart; beyond that they're far enough and get no gradient. Without the margin, the negative term would push everything to infinity. Its weakness is one absolute threshold for every pair.
An anchor a , a positive p (same identity) and a negative n . The negative must be farther than the positive by at least m , a relative constraint (FaceNet):
L = maxbig(0,\ d(a, p) - d(a, n) + mbig)
Triplets fall into three kinds by where the negative sits:
beginaligned easy:quad & d(a, n) > d(a, p) + m \\ semi-hard:quad & d(a, p) < d(a, n) < d(a, p) + m \\ hard:quad & d(a, n) < d(a, p) endaligned
Easy triplets have zero loss and teach nothing. Semi-hard ones are in the right order but inside the margin. Hard ones are in the wrong order.
The margin stops the model from being satisfied with a negative that's only barely farther away, and with normalized embeddings it sets the scale of the separation.
Mining matters: most random triplets are easy and contribute nothing. Mine negatives inside each batch (online), using batches built with several examples per identity so positives exist.

The hardest negatives can hurt: early in training they push the model towards a collapsed solution (every embedding at one point gives a constant loss of m ), and the very hardest are often label noise. FaceNet used semi-hard negatives; "batch-hard" with a soft margin is a common later variant.

A query q (the anchor) has one positive key k^+ among N candidate keys k_j , scored by similarity s and a temperature tau . It's softmax cross-entropy where the "classes" are the candidates and the label is the positive:
L = -logfracexpbig(s(q, k^+)/taubig)sum_j=1^Nexpbig(s(q, k_j)/taubig)

In-batch negatives. B matched pairs give a B times B similarity matrix S = Z_q Z_k^top/tau , where the rows of Z_q and Z_k are the normalized query and key embeddings. Each row is a B -way classification whose answer is the diagonal; the other B - 1 entries are negatives that cost nothing extra to compute.

In-batch negatives: with B pairs (q_i, k_i) , the labels are 0, dots, B - 1 and the loss is cross-entropy on the rows of S . CLIP averages the row loss (image to text) and the column loss (text to image). In recommendation, popular items show up as in-batch negatives far more often than rare ones, so apply the logQ correction (section 09).
NT-Xent (SimCLR): two augmented views of each of B images give 2B embeddings. Each one's positive is its other view; the other 2B - 2 are negatives. The self-similarity on the diagonal is masked out.

SigLIP replaces the row softmax with an independent sigmoid BCE on every cell of the B times B matrix (diagonal positive, the rest negative), with a learned temperature and bias. Each pair's loss no longer depends on the rest of the batch, which makes very large batches cheaper to shard and works well at small batch sizes too.
Why the temperature matters
As with any cross-entropy, the gradient with respect to each similarity is a softmax weight minus the label, scaled by 1/tau :
beginaligned fracpartial Lpartial s_j &= frac1tauBig(pi_j - mathbf 1[j = +]Big) \\ pi &= softmax(s / tau) endaligned
So each negative is pushed away in proportion to its softmax weight pi_j , and tau decides how that push is shared out:

Small tau : a sharp softmax, so nearly all the push goes to the hardest negatives (the most similar ones). Embeddings spread out more uniformly, but training is less stable and more hurt by false negatives: items that look like negatives but are really the same class.
Large tau : every negative is pushed about equally, so the loss stops caring which ones are confusing, and the embedding stays looser.

Scale: cosine similarities lie in [-1, 1] , so without a temperature the logits span only 2 units and the softmax can never become confident; the loss stays high. Typical values are 0.05 to 0.1, or learned: CLIP learns log(1/tau) and caps 1/tau at 100.
Why the batch size matters
More negatives make the task harder and put more hard negatives in every batch, which gives better representations. SimCLR used batches of thousands.

InfoNCE bounds the mutual information between query and key: I(q; k) ge log N - L . The bound can't exceed log N , so with few negatives the objective saturates. At initialization the loss is about log N .

Getting many negatives cheaply: MoCo keeps a queue of past keys from a slowly updated (momentum) encoder; multi-GPU training gathers embeddings from all devices before building S (otherwise each device only sees its own slice); memory banks store old embeddings. BYOL and SimSiam drop negatives entirely and avoid collapse with an asymmetric predictor and a stop-gradient.
False negatives grow with the batch (duplicates, same-class items). Supervised contrastive learning treats every same-label item as a positive; debiased variants correct the denominator.
Segmentation: Dice, IoU and Tversky

Per-pixel cross-entropy treats every pixel independently, so a small foreground object is outvoted by the background. Overlap losses score the predicted region as a whole. With predicted probabilities p_i and 0/1 ground truth g_i over the pixels, soft counts replace hard ones:
beginaligned TP &= sum_i p_i g_i \\ FP &= sum_i p_i (1 - g_i) \\ FN &= sum_i (1 - p_i)\, g_i \\ L_Dice &= 1 - frac2\,TP2\,TP + FP + FN \\ L_Tversky &= 1 - fracTPTP + a\,FP + b\,FN endaligned

Dice is a soft F1 (the denominator is sum_i p_i + sum_i g_i ). It's normalized by the region's size, so a small object counts as much as a large one, and it optimizes the evaluation metric directly. Add a small constant to the numerator and denominator so empty masks don't divide by zero. Soft IoU (Jaccard) is TP/(TP + FP + FN) .
Tversky weights the two error types separately: b > a penalizes missed pixels more and favours recall; setting both a and b to 0.5 gives Dice.

Dice plus cross-entropy is the usual default (nnU-Net). Dice's gradient is noisy when the region is tiny or empty and early in training; cross-entropy gives smooth per-pixel gradients, and Dice handles the imbalance.

L1 or smooth L1 on box offsets treats the four coordinates independently and isn't scale-invariant, while detectors are judged by IoU. Plain 1 - IoU is scale-invariant but has zero gradient when the boxes don't overlap. With predicted box A , target B , the smallest box C enclosing both, rho the distance between the two centres and c the diagonal of C :
beginaligned L_GIoU &= 1 - IoU + frac|C setminus (A cup B)||C| \\ L_DIoU &= 1 - IoU + fracrho^2c^2 endaligned
GIoU's extra term still has a gradient for disjoint boxes, pulling the prediction towards the target. DIoU pulls the centres together directly and converges faster; CIoU adds an aspect-ratio term.
The discriminator outputs a logit d and D = sigma(d) : a binary classifier trained with BCE, real as 1 and generated as 0. The original minimax game, with G the generator and n its noise input:
min_G max_D \; mathbb E_xbig[log D(x)big] + mathbb E_nbig[logbig(1 - D(G(n))big)big]

The minimax generator loss saturates, the same story as MSE through a sigmoid in section 03. Early on the discriminator rejects fakes easily, so for a fake d to -infty , and the generator's gradient with respect to d vanishes. The non-saturating loss has the generator maximize log D(G(n)) instead: the same fixed point, but a gradient near -1 exactly when the generator is worst. Minimax first, non-saturating second, as d to -infty :
beginaligned fracpartialpartial dlogbig(1 - sigma(d)big) &= -sigma(d) to 0 \\ fracpartialpartial dBig[-logsigma(d)Big] &= sigma(d) - 1 to -1 endaligned
With the optimal discriminator, the minimax objective is the Jensen–Shannon divergence between real and generated data, up to constants.

Wasserstein GAN: a critic with no sigmoid maximizes mathbb E[f(real)] - mathbb E[f(fake)] under a 1-Lipschitz constraint (weight clipping or a gradient penalty). It gives useful gradients even when the two distributions don't overlap, and its value tracks sample quality.
Hinge GAN (SAGAN, BigGAN): the discriminator minimizes mathbb E[max(0, 1 - d_real)] + mathbb E[max(0, 1 + d_fake)] and the generator minimizes -mathbb E[d_fake] .

A VAE maximizes the evidence lower bound (ELBO) on log p(x) , with an encoder q_phi(h mid x) over a latent code h , a decoder p_theta(x mid h) and a prior p(h) = mathcal N(0, I) . The loss is minus the ELBO: a reconstruction term plus a KL term.
beginaligned L &= -mathbb E_q_phi(h mid x)big[log p_theta(x mid h)big] \\ &quad + KLbig(q_phi(h mid x) Vert p(h)big) \\ KL &= tfrac12sum_jbig(mu_j^2 + sigma_j^2 - logsigma_j^2 - 1big) endaligned
The reconstruction term is MSE for a Gaussian decoder and per-pixel BCE for a Bernoulli one (section 01). The KL has the closed form above for a diagonal Gaussian encoder mathcal N(mu, diagsigma^2) .
Reparameterization: sampling isn't differentiable, so write h = mu + sigma odot epsilon with epsilon sim mathcal N(0, I) . The randomness moves into epsilon and gradients flow through mu and sigma .

Weighting the KL by beta trades reconstruction against a smoother latent space (β-VAE). A strong decoder can ignore h and drive the KL to 0 (posterior collapse); KL annealing or a minimum KL per dimension ("free bits") counters it.
beginaligned L_mean &= frac1Bsum_i=1^B ell_i \\ L_sum &= sum_i=1^B ell_i \\ &= B\,L_mean endaligned

With SGD the step is etanabla L . Under sum reduction the step grows with B , so changing the batch size silently changes the effective learning rate. Mean reduction keeps the gradient scale independent of B . The usual linear scaling rule (multiply B by k , try eta times k with warmup) is about the gradient becoming less noisy, and assumes mean reduction.

Adam is nearly invariant to a constant loss scale, since it divides by sqrtv . Mean vs sum matters much less, except through epsilon and through any L2 penalty added to the loss, whose relative strength changes with the scale of the data term.
Gradient accumulation over A micro-batches: divide each micro-batch loss by A , or the effective learning rate is A times too big.

Padding, unlabelled positions and prompt tokens shouldn't count. Set their targets to a sentinel (PyTorch's ignore_index, -100 by default): they get zero loss and zero gradient, and the mean divides by the number of real targets. By hand that's sum_i m_i ell_i / sum_i m_i for a 0/1 mask m . The trap is averaging over every position, padding included, which makes the loss depend on how much padding each batch had.

A language model is trained with token-level cross-entropy on the next token: logits of shape B times T times V , targets equal to the inputs shifted by one, flattened to (BT) times V . With a mask m :
L = -frac1sum_i,t m_itsum_i=1^Bsum_t=1^T m_it\,log qbig(y_it mid y_i,<tbig)
Per-token average (above): every token counts equally, so long sequences dominate. It's the standard language-modelling objective and matches perplexity.
Per-sequence average: average within each sequence, then across sequences. Every sequence counts equally, so the tokens of short sequences weigh more.

The accumulation trap: averaging per micro-batch and then over micro-batches isn't the per-token mean when micro-batches hold different numbers of tokens. Divide the summed loss by the total token count across all micro-batches. This bug has shipped in popular training libraries.

Supervised fine-tuning masks the prompt so only response tokens are trained. Seq2seq with teacher forcing feeds the gold previous token and applies cross-entropy at every target position. When the alignment between input and output is unknown (speech, handwriting), CTC sums the probability of every valid alignment with dynamic programming.

# logits: (B, T, V); targets: (B, T), pad and prompt positions = -100 logits, targets = logits[:, :-1], targets[:, 1:] # predict the next token logP = log_softmax(logits, axis=-1) # (B, T-1, V) mask = targets != -100 # (B, T-1) safe = where(mask, targets, 0) # any valid id; masked below nll = -take_along_axis(logP, safe[..., None], axis=-1)[..., 0] # (B, T-1) per_token = (nll * mask).sum() / mask.sum() # = ignore_index mean n_seq = mask.sum(1) # real tokens per row keep = n_seq > 0 # skip fully masked rows per_seq = ((nll * mask).sum(1)[keep] / n_seq[keep]).mean()

L = sum_k w_k L_k . The task losses have different units and scales (cross-entropy in nats, MSE in squared target units) and different gradient sizes on the shared layers, so equal weights let one task dominate, and grid-searching the weights is expensive.
Uncertainty weighting (Kendall et al., 2018) treats each task as having a learned noise level sigma_k , from the Gaussian NLL in section 01:
beginaligned L &= sum_k Big(frac12sigma_k^2\,L_k + logsigma_kBig) \\ &= sum_k Big(tfrac12\,e^-s_k\,L_k + tfrac12\,s_kBig) endaligned

Here s_k = logsigma_k^2 is what's actually learned. A task with a large loss gets a large sigma_k and so less weight; the logsigma_k term stops sigma_k from growing forever. For fixed L_k the optimum is sigma_k^2 = L_k , so each task's effective weight is about 1/L_k : the method balances tasks by their loss scale. Learning s_k rather than sigma_k keeps it stable.
GradNorm tunes the weights so each task's gradient norm on the last shared layer moves towards a common target, raised for tasks that are training more slowly.
PCGrad ("gradient surgery"): when two tasks' gradients conflict (negative cosine), project one onto the plane normal to the other before summing.
Strong simple baselines: divide each loss by its initial value or a running mean, then tune a few weights.
Extra terms that help the main task train and are usually dropped at inference:
deep supervision (Inception's side classifiers, extra outputs in U-Net++), which injects gradient into middle layers;
the load-balancing loss in mixture-of-experts models, which pushes the router to spread tokens across experts;
regularizers written as losses: weight decay, the VAE's KL to the prior, consistency terms between two dropout passes;
self-supervised side tasks (masked tokens, next-state prediction in RL) next to a supervised head.
Keep their weights small enough that the main loss's gradient dominates, and check they don't conflict with it.

The loss is what the optimizer minimizes: differentiable, ideally proper, matched to the noise. The metric is what you report and decide on: accuracy, F1, AUC, NDCG, cost. They're often different, and that's fine.

They can disagree. Validation loss rising while validation accuracy still rises is common: the model flips more borderline cases to correct while becoming very confident on the ones it still gets wrong, whose -log p explodes. Early-stop on the metric that matters, and recalibrate if you need probabilities.

Match the loss to the metric where you can: an MAE metric wants an MAE or Huber loss (MSE predicts the mean, not the median); a quantile metric wants pinball loss; a ranking metric wants a pairwise or listwise loss; probability quality wants log loss.
Why you can't train on accuracy

Accuracy, frac1Nsum_i mathbf 1[argmax_k z_ik = y_i] , is piecewise constant in the weights: a tiny change almost never flips an argmax, so the gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined where it jumps. Gradient descent gets no signal. F1, precision at k , AUC and NDCG have the same problem, because they depend on thresholds or sort orders. The options:

Surrogate losses: a smooth proxy or upper bound. Cross-entropy for accuracy (the margin figure above). For AUC, which is P(s^+ > s^-) for a random positive and negative, there are two routes. Replacing the indicator mathbf 1[s^+ > s^-] with sigma(s^+ - s^-) gives a soft AUC to maximize, but it's non-convex and saturates like MSE on a sigmoid. Minimizing -logsigma(s^+ - s^-) instead is the pairwise logistic (RankNet) loss, a convex upper bound on the mis-ordering indicator (in base 2). "Soft F1" computes true and false positives from probabilities instead of hard predictions. LambdaRank for NDC
Post-hoc tuning: train with cross-entropy, then choose the threshold that maximizes F1 on validation data. This captures most of the gain.
Policy gradient (REINFORCE): treat the output as a sampled action and the metric R as a reward:
nabla_theta\,mathbb Ebig[R(hat y)big] = mathbb EBig[big(R(hat y) - bbig)\,nabla_thetalog q_theta(hat y)Big]

Both expectations are over outputs sampled from the model, hat y sim q_theta . It works for any black-box reward (BLEU or CIDEr in self-critical sequence training, a learned reward model in RLHF), but its variance is high: it needs a baseline b (the greedy output's reward, or a learned value) and usually cross-entropy pretraining first.
Relaxations such as Gumbel-softmax or differentiable sorting are another route when a discrete step sits inside the model.
K -class cross-entropy, small random init
Much higher means the initial logits are too large: confidently wrong from step 0. Check the last layer's init.
BCE, output bias set to logfracpi1 - pi (base rate pi )
-pilogpi - (1 - pi)log(1 - pi)
With a zero bias it starts at log 2 and wastes early steps learning the base rate.
InfoNCE with N candidates
Much lower at the start suggests leakage between anchor and positive.
MSE predicting a constant c
Standardize the target so this is about 1.
perplexity e^L ; uniform over V gives V

The floor isn't zero. With label noise or genuinely ambiguous inputs, the best possible expected cross-entropy is the conditional entropy H(y mid x) ; with label smoothing it's the smoothed target's entropy; for MSE it's the noise variance. A loss that plateaus above zero may be at its floor, not stuck.

Training loss above validation loss isn't by itself a bug: dropout and augmentation are on in training and off in evaluation, and the training loss is often averaged over an epoch while the model improved.
NaN: log 0 (use logits), float16 overflow, a learning rate that's too high, exploding gradients, or a masked mean over an empty mask.
Loss falls but the metric doesn't move: check the mask and label alignment (training on padding?), or the model may only be growing its confidence on examples it already gets right.
Before anything else, overfit one small batch: the loss should reach its floor.

Softmax cross-entropy, forward and backward

# Z: (B, K) logits y: (B,) integer class ids def softmax_ce(Z, y): B = Z.shape[0] m = Z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True) # (B, 1) row max lse = m + log(exp(Z - m).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) # (B, 1) logP = Z - lse # (B, K) log-probs loss = -logP[arange(B), y].mean() # mean over the batch P = exp(logP) # softmax, no overflow dZ = P.copy() dZ[arange(B), y] -= 1 # P - Y, Y one-hot dZ /= B # from the mean return loss, dZ # dZ: (B, K) # into the last layer Z = H @ W + b, H: (B, d) W: (d, K) dW = H.T @ dZ # (d, K) db = dZ.sum(axis=0) # (K,) dH = dZ @ W.T # (B, d), sent to the layer below # soft targets T
Binary cross-entropy with logits

# z: (B,) logits y: (B,) in 0, 1 pw: weight on positives def bce_with_logits(z, y, pw=1.0): sp_pos = maximum(z, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(z))) # softplus(z) = -log(1 - p) sp_neg = sp_pos - z # softplus(-z) = -log p loss = (pw * y * sp_neg + (1 - y) * sp_pos).mean() p = sigmoid(z) dz = (pw * y * (p - 1) + (1 - y) * p) / len(z) # (p - y)/B if pw = 1 return loss, dz def sigmoid(z): # never exponentiates a large positive e = exp(-abs(z)) return where(z >= 0, 1 / (1 + e), e / (1 + e))
Focal loss (binary, from logits)

# z: (N,) logits y: (N,) in 0, 1 def focal_loss(z, y, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.25): p = sigmoid(z) ce = maximum(z, 0) - z * y + log1p(exp(-abs(z))) # BCE per example p_t = y * p + (1 - y) * (1 - p) # prob. of the true class a_t = y * alpha + (1 - y) * (1 - alpha) loss = a_t * (1 - p_t) ** gamma * ce # easy examples -> about 0 return loss.sum() / max(1, y.sum()) # RetinaNet: per positive # backward: autograd, or per example in the true-class logit z_t: # -a_t * (1 - p_t)**gamma * ((1 - p_t) + gamma * p_t * ce) (log p_t = -ce)
InfoNCE with in-batch negatives

# Zq: (B, d) queries (anchors) Zk: (B, d) keys; row i of Zq matches row i of Zk def info_nce(Zq, Zk, tau=0.07, symmetric=True): Zq = Zq / norm(Zq, axis=1, keepdims=True) # unit vectors: dot = cosine Zk = Zk / norm(Zk, axis=1, keepdims=True) S = Zq @ Zk.T / tau # (B, B) similarity logits labels = arange(len(Zq)) # row i's positive is column i loss = cross_entropy(S, labels) # each row: a B-way softmax if symmetric: # CLIP: columns too loss = (loss + cross_entropy(S.T, labels)) / 2 return loss # about log B at init # row term's gradient: dS = (softmax(S, axis=1) - I) / B, then 1/tau into Zq @ Zk
Answer out loud first, then open the answer.
1Derive MSE from maximum likelihood. What does it assume, and what does the model end up predicting? What about MAE?
Assume y mid x sim mathcal N(hat y, sigma^2) with fixed sigma . Then:
beginaligned -log p(y mid x) &= frac(y - hat y)^22sigma^2 + const \\ argmin_hat y\ mathbb Ebig[(y - hat y)^2big] &= mathbb E[y mid x] endaligned

It assumes symmetric, light-tailed noise with one variance everywhere. It predicts the conditional mean, and that holds for any noise distribution; Gaussianity only makes it the most efficient choice. MAE is the Laplace likelihood and predicts the conditional median. Pinball loss at level tau predicts the tau -quantile. (01)
2Your regression target has outliers. What do you do?

First decide whether they're errors (fix or drop them) or real (keep them). For real heavy tails, use a loss whose pull is capped: Huber (MSE with its gradient clipped at delta , with delta set from the residual scale), MAE if the median is what you want, or log-cosh if you need a smooth second derivative. A log transform also tames skewed targets, but then MSE predicts the geometric mean, which is below the mean, so correct it if predictions get summed. If the real question is a percentile, use pinball loss. (02)
3What loss for daily order counts? For spend per customer, where most customers spend nothing?

Counts: Poisson with a log link, L = e^f - y f , gradient mu - y . It keeps predictions positive, makes effects multiplicative and assumes variance equals mean; use negative binomial if the data is overdispersed and you need intervals, and an exposure offset for rates. Zero-inflated spend: Tweedie with 1 < p < 2 , a point mass at zero plus a continuous positive part, with gradient mu^1-p(mu - y) . Plain MSE would predict negatives, ignore that variance grows with the mean, and be dominated by big spenders. (02)
4Why does softmax with cross-entropy give p - y at the logits?
The softmax Jacobian is partial p_i/partial z_j = p_i(delta_ij - p_j) . The loss contributes -y_i/p_i , so the p_i cancels:
beginaligned fracpartial Lpartial z_j &= -sum_i fracy_ip_i\,p_i\,(delta_ij - p_j) \\ &= -y_j + p_jsum_i y_i \\ &= p_j - y_j endaligned

Equivalently, L = -z_c + logsum_k e^z_k , and the gradient of log-sum-exp is the softmax. The deeper reason is that softmax is the canonical link of the categorical distribution; every GLM with its canonical link has "prediction minus target" as its gradient. It works for any soft target that sums to 1. (04)
5Why not use MSE for classification?

Through a sigmoid, MSE's gradient is (p - y)\,p(1 - p) . The p(1 - p) factor vanishes when the output saturates, so a confidently wrong example gets almost no gradient, exactly where learning matters most; cross-entropy's p - y is near pm 1 there. MSE is also non-convex in the logit (the curvature flips sign at p = 1/3 for y = 1 ), its penalty for a confident mistake is bounded, and it's the wrong likelihood for a 0/1 label. As a metric on probabilities (the Brier score) it's fine. (03)
6What goes wrong if you forget the softmax, apply it twice, or compute the loss from clamped probabilities?

Probabilities into CrossEntropyLoss: a double softmax. The inputs lie in [0, 1] , so the true class can reach at most e/(e + K - 1) ; the loss has a high floor and the gradients are tiny. Slow training, meaningless probabilities.
Logits into NLLLoss with no log-softmax: the loss is -z_c , unbounded below, so it diverges to minus infinity.
Softmax, then log: log 0 gives -infty and then NaN. Use log-softmax (log-sum-exp).

Clamping p to [varepsilon, 1 - varepsilon] : clamp has zero derivative outside the range, so the most confidently wrong examples get exactly zero gradient. Frameworks take logits so the loss is computed stably and the gradient is exactly p - y . (05)
7Multi-class vs multi-label: what output layer and loss?

Exactly one label: softmax over K with cross-entropy; probabilities compete and sum to 1; predict with argmax. Any subset: K independent sigmoids with a BCE per label; each probability is separate, there's an implicit "none", and each label gets its own threshold. Mutually exclusive groups within a multi-label problem get one softmax per group. (04)
8How are entropy, cross-entropy and KL related? Forward vs reverse KL?
beginaligned H(p, q) &= -sum_k p_klog q_k \\ &= H(p) + KL(p Vert q) endaligned

The entropy of the data doesn't depend on the model, so minimizing cross-entropy is maximum likelihood is minimizing KL(data Vert model) . Forward KL averages over the data, so the model must cover every mode: mass-covering. Reverse KL averages over the model, so it avoids regions where the data is thin and locks onto a mode: mode-seeking, as in variational inference and the KL penalty in RLHF. KL isn't symmetric, so it isn't a distance. (06)
9What loss should a K -class classifier show at step 0, and what does it mean if it's far higher?

With small random weights the logits are near zero, the softmax is uniform, and the loss is -log(1/K) = log K (perplexity K ). Much higher means the initial logits are large, so the model starts confidently wrong and wastes steps undoing it: scale down the last layer's init. For binary problems, set the output bias to the log-odds of the base rate so the starting loss is the base rate's entropy instead of log 2 . The floor isn't 0 either: label noise sets it at H(y mid x) . (13)
10You have a 1-in-1,000 positive rate. How do you handle it in the loss?
Cross-entropy doesn't bias the probabilities under imbalance; the real issues are a gradient dominated by easy negatives and a wrong default threshold. Options:
Class weights or pos_weight: they multiply the predicted odds by w , which is a threshold shift; ranking is nearly unchanged.
Resampling: keeping a fraction rho of the negatives multiplies the odds by 1/rho ; correct with logit p = logit p_s + logrho . Balanced batches are steadier than huge weights for neural nets.
Focal loss when there are huge numbers of easy negatives.
In practice: often train unweighted, calibrate, pick the threshold from costs, and evaluate with PR-AUC or cost rather than accuracy. (07)
11Explain focal loss. What do gamma and alpha do?
FL = -\,alpha_t\,(1 - p_t)^gammalog p_t

(1 - p_t)^gamma down-weights well-classified examples ( p_t near 1) of either class, so the loss and gradient concentrate on hard and misclassified ones; gamma = 0 is cross-entropy and 2 is typical. It was built for one-stage detection, where around 100,000 easy background anchors would swamp the loss. alpha is a class weight; with gamma = 2 , RetinaNet's best was 0.25 on the rare class, because gamma had already removed most of the negatives' loss. It's not a proper scoring rule, so check calibration. (07)
12Label smoothing vs focal loss?

Label smoothing changes the target to (1 - varepsilon)y + varepsilon/K for every example. It caps the logit gap at logbig(1 + K(1 - varepsilon)/varepsilonbig) , stops logits growing forever, reduces over-confidence and tightens class clusters. Focal loss changes each example's weight by difficulty, so easy examples nearly vanish; it's for an easy majority swamping the gradient. Smoothing hurts distillation and anything needing real confidence; focal loss pulls probabilities towards 0.5. Both lower confidence, and neither replaces measuring calibration. (08)
13What is calibration, how do you measure it, and how does temperature scaling fix it without changing accuracy?

Calibrated means that of the cases scored p , a fraction p are positive. Measure it with a reliability diagram and ECE, the count-weighted gap between accuracy and confidence across confidence bins, alongside log loss or Brier. Deep networks are often over-confident because cross-entropy keeps rewarding larger logits. Temperature scaling fits one scalar T on held-out data to minimize the NLL of softmax(z/T) . Dividing every logit by the same positive number never changes the argmax, so accuracy is identical while confidence is softened. (08)
14In knowledge distillation, why use a temperature, and why multiply the soft loss by T^2 ?

At T = 1 the teacher's probabilities are nearly one-hot, so the information about which wrong classes resemble the right one sits in tiny probabilities that carry no gradient. Softening with T > 1 exposes it. The soft term's gradient, and its high-temperature limit, are:
beginaligned fracpartial\,KLpartial z &= fracq^T - p^TT \\ &approx fracz - vK T^2 endaligned
So it shrinks like 1/T^2 ; multiplying by T^2 keeps its weight relative to the hard-label term fixed as T changes. At very high T , distillation becomes logit matching with squared error. (06)
15Hinge vs logistic loss. Why doesn't an SVM give probabilities?

Both are convex surrogates for the 0–1 loss as functions of the margin m = yz . Hinge, max(0, 1 - m) , is exactly zero beyond the margin, so only support vectors shape the solution, giving sparse, margin-maximizing behaviour. Logistic, log(1 + e^-m) , never reaches zero, keeps nudging every point and is a likelihood. Hinge's population minimizer is sign(2p - 1) , the best decision rather than the probability, so SVM scores need Platt scaling to become probabilities. (09)
16Why can't you train directly on accuracy, F1 or NDCG? What do you do instead?

They're piecewise constant in the weights: small weight changes almost never flip a prediction or a sort order, so the gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the jumps. Instead: train a smooth surrogate (cross-entropy for accuracy, pairwise logistic for AUC, LambdaRank for NDCG, soft F1), tune the threshold on validation data to maximize the metric, or use REINFORCE with the metric as a reward and a baseline to cut variance, as in sequence-level training and RLHF. (13)
17Triplet loss: what is the margin for, and why do hard negatives matter? Can they hurt?

L = maxbig(0,\ d(a, p) - d(a, n) + mbig) . The margin demands that the negative be farther than the positive by m , not just barely farther, which sets the scale of the separation. Most random triplets already satisfy it and give zero gradient, so you mine hard or semi-hard negatives within the batch. The very hardest negatives early in training can collapse the embedding to a point and are often label noise, which is why FaceNet used semi-hard ones. (10)
18Why is InfoNCE's temperature important, and why does batch size matter?

InfoNCE is softmax cross-entropy over similarities divided by tau , and its gradient pushes each negative in proportion to its softmax weight. Small tau concentrates the push on the hardest negatives: more uniform embeddings, but less stable and more sensitive to false negatives. Large tau treats all negatives alike. Since cosine similarities lie in [-1, 1] , without a small tau the softmax can't get confident at all. Batch size sets the number of negatives: more and harder negatives per step, and the mutual-information bound log N - L is capped at log N . Hence large batches, MoCo's queue, an
19Mean vs sum reduction: what changes when you switch? And how should a padded sequence loss be averaged?

Sum makes the gradient, and so SGD's effective learning rate, grow with batch size; mean keeps it independent of B . Adam is mostly insensitive to the loss scale, apart from epsilon and L2 terms. With gradient accumulation, divide by the number of micro-batches. For sequences, mask padding with ignore_index and divide by the number of real tokens, never by all positions. Per-token averaging weights long sequences more; per-sequence averaging weights each sequence equally. With accumulation, divide by the total tokens across all micro-batches. (12)
20How do you weight the losses in a multi-task model?

Task losses differ in units, scale and gradient size, so fixed equal weights let one task dominate. Simple baselines normalize each loss by its initial value or a running mean. Uncertainty weighting learns s_k = logsigma_k^2 per task and minimizes sum_k big(tfrac12 e^-s_kL_k + tfrac12 s_kbig) , giving each task a weight of about 1/L_k . GradNorm balances the tasks' gradient norms on the shared layers; PCGrad projects away conflicting gradient components. (12)
21How does training a neural network relate to maximum likelihood? What is the network assuming about the data?
Minimizing the usual losses is maximum-likelihood estimation: the network outputs a distribution's parameters, and the loss is that distribution's negative log-likelihood.
Assuming i.i.d. examples, the dataset's likelihood is a product over examples, and its negative log is a sum, which mini-batch SGD can estimate:
beginaligned hattheta &= argmax_theta prod_i p_theta(y_i mid x_i) \\ &= argmin_theta sum_i -log p_theta(y_i mid x_i) endaligned
The head fixes the distribution, and the distribution fixes the loss:
linear output → Gaussian with fixed variance → MSE (predicts the mean);
sigmoid → Bernoulli → BCE;
softmax → categorical → cross-entropy;
softmax at every position → autoregressive language model → token-level cross-entropy.
Outputs independent given the input: per-pixel MSE blurs uncertain images for this reason.
Weight decay adds a Gaussian prior, which turns MLE into MAP.
Is every deep-learning loss MLE? No. VAEs and diffusion models maximize a bound on the likelihood, GANs use none, and triplet, hinge and contrastive losses are margin objectives.
Why are big networks overconfident? The NLL keeps rewarding larger logits on training data.
What does the CLT have to do with it? It motivates Gaussian noise, and it makes mini-batch gradients roughly Gaussian with variance shrinking as 1/B .
22Where do cross-entropy and the other losses come from? How do you pick a loss for a new target?
Each loss is the negative log-likelihood of an assumed distribution for y mid x ; pick the distribution that matches how the target is generated, and the loss follows.
Binary label: a Bernoulli with p = sigma(z) gives BCE, -ylog p - (1-y)log(1-p) . That is logistic regression.
One of K classes: a categorical with p = softmax(z) gives cross-entropy, -log p_y .
Real value, symmetric noise: Gaussian gives MSE (predicts the mean); Laplace gives MAE (predicts the median), more robust to outliers.
Counts: Poisson with a log link, loss mu - ylogmu ; predictions stay positive and the variance grows with the mean.
Positive, skewed amounts (spend, claim size): Gamma or Tweedie with a log link.

Why this matters: the distribution decides what the optimum predicts (mean, median, probability), how hard outliers pull, and whether predictions respect the target's range. A mismatched loss still trains, but it estimates the wrong quantity, for example a mean when the business needs a quantile. Regularization fits the same frame: a Gaussian prior on the weights adds L2, a Laplace prior adds L1. (01)
Gaussian prior on weights
+lambdalVertthetarVert_2^2

beginaligned MSE: partial L/partial hat y &= hat y - y \\ Huber: partial L/partial hat y &= clip(hat y - y, -delta, delta) \\ Pinball: partial L/partial hat y &= -tau or 1 - tau \\ Poisson: partial L/partial f &= mu - y \\ BCE, CE: partial L/partial z &= p - y \\ softmax: J &= diag(p) - p\,p^top endaligned
beginaligned m &= max_j z_j \\ logtextstylesum_j e^z_j &= m + logtextstylesum_j e^z_j - m \\ BCE(z, y) &= max(z, 0) - y z + logbig(1 + e^-|z|big) endaligned
beginaligned H(p, q) &= H(p) + KL(p Vert q) \\ PPL &= exp(mean token CE) \\ initial CE &approx log K endaligned
Imbalance and calibration

beginaligned weight w &Rightarrow odds times w \\ logit p &= logit p_s + logrho \\ FL &= -alpha_t (1 - p_t)^gammalog p_t \\ y^LS &= (1 - varepsilon)\,y + varepsilon/K \\ temperature scaling: p &= softmax(z / T^*) endaligned
Margin, ranking, contrastive

beginaligned hinge &= max(0,\ 1 - y z) \\ RankNet &= logbig(1 + e^-(s_i - s_j)big) \\ triplet &= maxbig(0,\ d(a, p) - d(a, n) + mbig) \\ InfoNCE &= -logfrace^s^+/tausum_j e^s_j/tau \\ DPO &= -logsigmabig(hat r_w - hat r_lbig) endaligned
Segmentation, boxes, generative

beginaligned L_Dice &= 1 - frac2sum_i p_i g_isum_i p_i + sum_i g_i \\ L_GIoU &= 1 - IoU + frac|C setminus (A cup B)||C| \\ L_VAE &= -mathbb E_qbig[log p_theta(x mid h)big] + KL(q_phi Vert p) endaligned
Which loss for which problem
An average (price, amount)
MSE on standardized targets
A median, P90 or an interval
Yes/no with a probability
Softmax cross-entropy (plus label smoothing for large K )
A sigmoid and BCE per label
Rare positives, many easy negatives
Unweighted CE and a cost-based threshold first; then weights, balanced sampling or focal loss if needed, and recalibrate
Segmentation with small objects
Dice plus CE (Tversky to favour recall)
Bradley–Terry reward model, or DPO
Pairwise (RankNet, BPR) or LambdaRank
InfoNCE with in-batch negatives, or triplet
A smaller copy of a big model
Distillation: CE plus T^2\,KL at temperature T

notes.title: Convolutional neural networks
notes.desc: Why convolution, shapes and costs, receptive fields, pooling, 1×1 and depthwise convs, architectures, how convolution is computed (im2col, FFT, Winograd), upsampling and U-Net, CNN vs ViT.

sections.t: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
The backward pass is also a convolution
ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
Winograd: fewer multiplications for small kernels

chunks.x: Convolutional neural networks · Deepam Minda

A conv layer is a dense layer with two constraints: each output reads only a small patch (locality), and the same filter is used at every position (weight sharing). Parameters drop from (HWC_in)(HWC_out) to k^2 C_in C_out , and the layer becomes translation equivariant. That built-in bias is why CNNs learn from far less data than dense nets on images.

The output size counts where the window can start; the parameters, about k^2 C_in C_out , don't depend on resolution, while compute and memory grow with the output's area. The receptive field grows by k - 1 times the product of earlier strides at every layer.

Libraries rarely run the naive loops. im2col + GEMM unfolds patches into a matrix and does one big matrix multiply (fast, but up to k^2 times the memory). FFT convolution uses the convolution theorem, mathcal F(x circledast w) = mathcal F(x) cdot mathcal F(w) (circular convolution; zero-pad for the ordinary kind): O(n^2 log n) instead of O(n^2 k^2) , worth it only for large kernels. Winograd cuts a 3×3 conv's multiplications by 2.25–4×. cuDNN times them and picks one.

To get H times W back: transposed convolution (the gradient of a conv; checkerboard artifacts when k isn't divisible by s ), resize then conv, max-unpooling with saved indices, pixel shuffle, or dilated convs that avoid downsampling. Skip connections (U-Net) supply the fine detail from before the downsampling, which no upsampler can recreate.

Architectures each add one idea: stacked 3×3s (VGG), cheap 1×1 reductions (Inception), residuals that fix the degradation problem (ResNet), depthwise separable convs at about 1/k^2 the cost (MobileNet), compound scaling (EfficientNet), transformer-era design in a pure CNN (ConvNeXt).

CNN vs ViT: a CNN's locality and equivariance are free knowledge with little data and cost linear in pixels; a ViT is global from layer 1 and scales better with data, but costs quadratic in tokens and needs large pretraining. Hybrids and ConvNeXt sit in between.
Take a layer that maps an image with C_in channels to a same-sized map with C_out channels. Count its weights (biases ignored) under three designs, each adding one constraint to the one before:
beginaligned P_dense &= (H W C_in) cdot (H W C_out) \\ P_local &= H W cdot k^2 C_in C_out \\ P_conv &= k^2 C_in C_out endaligned

In words: a dense layer connects every output to every input. A locally connected layer lets each output read only a k times k patch, which divides the count by HW/k^2 . A convolution also uses the same patch weights at all HW positions, which divides it by another HW . Altogether the count falls by (HW)^2/k^2 , and it no longer depends on the image size at all.
Each constraint is an assumption about images, an inductive bias built in before any data is seen:

Locality. Nearby pixels are strongly related and distant ones weakly, so the useful low-level features (edges, corners, textures) are local. Without it, a dense layer must learn from data that most of its weights should be zero, which costs parameters, samples and compute.

Weight sharing. A pattern means the same thing wherever it appears, so the detector learned in one place should be reused everywhere. Without it, the network must see each pattern at each position to learn it there.
Hierarchy. Stacking layers composes local patterns into larger ones: edges, then parts, then objects. Each layer's view of the image grows (section 03).
Sharing gives translation equivariance: shift the input and the feature map shifts the same way.
(T_Delta x) star w = T_Delta (x star w)

In words: T_Delta shifts an image by Delta pixels and star is the conv layer's operation. Convolving the shifted image gives the shifted feature map. It holds exactly for stride 1 away from the borders; strides and pooling break it (section 04).

A useful way to see it: written as a matrix acting on the flattened image, a conv layer is a dense layer whose matrix is mostly zeros (locality) with repeated entries along its diagonals (sharing): a doubly block-Toeplitz matrix. That view explains the backward pass and the transposed convolution later (section 09).

The trade-off. When the assumptions hold, they're free knowledge: less data, less overfitting, any input size. When they don't, they hurt. Shuffle every image's pixels with one fixed permutation and a dense net trains exactly as well as before (it just permutes its weights), while a CNN collapses, because its windows now hold unrelated pixels. The same goes for table columns, or a form where the absolute position of a field is the signal. Equivariance also covers only shifts: not rotation, scale or lighting, which have to come from data augmentation (section 10).
Where convolutions fit: any grid with local, position-independent structure. That means images (2D), audio and time series (1D convolutions along time), video and volumetric scans (3D).

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: beginaligned y[i, j] &= sum_u, v w[u, v]\; x[i + u,\, j + v] \\ (x * w)[i, j] &= sum_u, v w[u, v]\; x[i - u,\, j - v] endaligned

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: In words: the first line is what a CNN layer computes, the second the mathematical convolution. The true convolution flips the kernel (upside down and left to right) before sliding it; a CNN layer slides it unflipped, which is cross-correlation. Since the kernel is learned, a network that needs the flipped pattern just learns flipped weights, so for training it makes no difference.

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: It does matter in three places: porting weights to or from a signal-processing routine, FFT convolution (section 08), and the backward pass, where the input's gradient turns out to be a true convolution.

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs

chunks.x: In words: d(k - 1) + 1 is the kernel's effective span. Padding makes the input H + 2p long, so the window's first cell can start at 0, s, 2s, dots up to H + 2p - span . The fraction counts the steps after the first start and the +1 counts the first. The floor drops a last window that would hang off the edge, so those last rows of the input are silently never used. With d = 1 it's the familiar lfloor (H + 2p - k)/s rfloor + 1 .

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: Why pad: without it, every layer shrinks the map and border pixels fall inside fewer windows than central ones, so they barely influence the output. Padding keeps the size, so networks can be deep.

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: What it costs: zeros are fake data. They create an artificial edge at the border, and a deep network can use that edge to work out absolute position, which breaks pure translation equivariance. Reflect or replicate padding avoids the fake edge.

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: Why kernels are odd: an odd kernel has a centre pixel, so “same” padding is symmetric. An even kernel needs uneven padding and shifts the map by half a pixel.

chunks.x: beginaligned params &= C_out cdot fracC_ing cdot k^2 + C_out \\ MACs &= N cdot H_out W_out cdot C_out cdot fracC_ing cdot k^2 \\ activations &= N cdot C_out cdot H_out W_out endaligned

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: In words: each filter has C_in/g times k times k weights and a bias. Each output value costs one multiply-add (MAC) per filter weight, and there are N C_out H_out W_out outputs. FLOPs are about twice the MACs. The activations are what the backward pass must store.

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: The consequence: parameters don't depend on resolution, but compute and memory do. Early layers (high resolution, few channels) dominate activation memory; late layers (low resolution, many channels) dominate the parameters; compute is spread roughly evenly, because the usual stage design halves H and W and doubles the channels, which keeps the cost per layer level:

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: tfracH2 cdot tfracW2 cdot (2C)^2 k^2 = H W C^2 k^2

chunks.h: The operation: shapes, sizes and costs
chunks.x: In words: a quarter of the positions times four times the channel pairs is the same number of multiply-adds.

chunks.h: The backward pass is also a convolution
chunks.x: Write delta = partial L / partial y for the gradient arriving at the output, with subscripts for indices (stride 1, no padding, and delta is zero outside its range):

chunks.h: The backward pass is also a convolution
chunks.x: beginaligned fracpartial Lpartial w_ocuv &= sum_n, i, j delta_noij\; x_n,\, c,\, i+u,\, j+v \\ fracpartial Lpartial x_ncab &= sum_o, u, v delta_n,\, o,\, a-u,\, b-v\; w_ocuv \\ fracpartial Lpartial b_o &= sum_n, i, j delta_noij endaligned

chunks.h: The backward pass is also a convolution
chunks.x: Weights: a shared weight is used at every position, so its gradient sums one term per position (summed, not averaged). That sum is the input cross-correlated with the output gradient.

chunks.h: The backward pass is also a convolution
chunks.x: Input: each input pixel fed every window that covered it, so its gradient collects from all of them. The minus signs make it a true convolution: the output gradient, zero-padded “full”, convolved with the kernel. This is exactly the transposed convolution of section 09 (the formula above is the stride-1 case; with stride s it's a stride- s transposed conv).

chunks.h: The backward pass is also a convolution
chunks.x: Pooling: max pooling sends the gradient only to the maximum in each window; average pooling splits it equally.

chunks.h: The backward pass is also a convolution
chunks.x: Why it matters: a training step runs three convolution-shaped computations per layer (forward, weight gradient, input gradient), so the fast algorithms of section 08 pay off three times.

A unit's receptive field is the patch of the input that can affect it. Track two numbers layer by layer: the field r , and the jump j , the distance in input pixels between neighbouring units at that layer.
beginaligned r_l &= r_l-1 + (k_l - 1)\, d_l\, j_l-1 \\ j_l &= j_l-1\, s_l \\ r_0 &= j_0 = 1 endaligned
In words: each layer widens the view by its kernel's extra span, (k - 1)d , measured in units of the current jump; then its stride multiplies the jump. Pooling layers count as layers. Unrolled:
r_L = 1 + sum_l=1^L (k_l - 1)\, d_l prod_m=1^l-1 s_m
Two stacked 3×3 layers along one row. Each layer-1 unit sees 3 input pixels; the layer-2 unit reads 3 overlapping layer-1 units, so it sees 5. Each stride-1 layer adds k - 1 = 2 .
L stacked stride-1 3×3 layers: 2L + 1 . The field grows only linearly with depth.
A stride-2 layer doubles the jump, so every later layer adds twice as much. Downsampling early is the cheap way to see far.
Dilations 1, 2, 4, dots, 2^L-1 with 3×3 kernels give 2^L+1 - 1 : exponential growth at full resolution.

The formula gives the theoretical field: what can possibly matter. The effective field is what does. A central input pixel reaches a top unit through many more paths than a pixel at the edge of the field. With the paths weighted equally, the number of paths to each pixel is the kernel's footprint convolved with itself L times, which by the central limit theorem is a bell curve:
beginaligned theoretical radius &propto L \\ effective radius &propto sqrtL endaligned

In words: the influence (the gradient of the unit with respect to each input pixel) is concentrated in a Gaussian-shaped blob whose width grows like sqrt L , so the effective share of the theoretical field shrinks like 1/sqrt L (Luo et al., 2016). Training widens it somewhat. So “the receptive field covers the whole image” doesn't mean the unit actually uses the whole image.

Why it matters: a unit can't use information outside its field. A classifier's top units must see the whole object; a segmentation network needs context at every pixel (is this grey patch road or river?). Too small a field and the network can't tell apart things that differ only in their surroundings.
More compute and depth; the effective field grows only like sqrt L
Downsampling (stride, pooling)
Multiplies every later layer's growth
Loses resolution, which dense prediction needs back (section 09)
Full-resolution maps are expensive; gridding artifacts
7×7 depthwise (ConvNeXt), even 31×31 (RepLKNet)
Cost grows with k^2 , cheap only if depthwise
Global pooling, squeeze-and-excitation, attention blocks
Attention costs quadratic in positions
beginaligned y_max[i, j] &= max_0 le u, v < k\; x[s i + u,\, s j + v] \\ y_avg[i, j] &= frac1k^2 sum_0 le u, v < k x[s i + u,\, s j + v] endaligned

In words: for each channel separately, summarize each k times k window by its largest value or its mean. There are no parameters and no mixing across channels; the output size follows the same formula as a conv. The usual 2×2 window with stride 2 halves H and W .
Why pool: downsampling makes every later layer cheaper and grows the receptive field faster, and a small shift inside a window doesn't change its maximum, which gives some local invariance.
Equivariance vs invariance
beginaligned equivariant:quad f(T x) &= T f(x) \\ invariant:quad g(T x) &= g(x) endaligned

In words: an equivariant map moves with its input; an invariant one ignores the move. Feature maps should be equivariant (the edge moved, so its response should move); a class label should be invariant (a cat that moves is still a cat). Conv layers are equivariant, pooling makes small local shifts invariant, and a global pool at the end makes the whole classifier roughly invariant. Detection and segmentation need to know where things are, so they keep equivariant spatial maps to the end.

Max vs average: max asks “is the feature anywhere in this window?” and passes the gradient only to the winner; average keeps the total response, blurs, and spreads the gradient evenly. Max dominated inside classic CNNs.

Strided conv instead: a stride-2 convolution downsamples with learned weights (the “all-convolutional” net; most ResNet downsampling; ConvNeXt's separate downsampling layers). It costs parameters but chooses what to keep.
Aliasing: CNNs aren't really shift-invariant
Keeping every s -th sample can only represent frequencies below a limit (the sampling theorem):
f_max = frac12s \ cycles per pixel

In words: anything that oscillates faster than one full cycle per two kept samples ( 2s input pixels) can't be represented, and instead of vanishing it folds back as a false slow pattern (aliasing, the moiré effect).

Max pooling and strided convs subsample without smoothing first, so fine detail aliases. The result: shift an image by one pixel and the subsampled grid lands on different samples, and a classifier's output can change noticeably (Azulay and Weiss, 2019). The fix is the one signal processing has always used: low-pass filter before subsampling. BlurPool (Zhang, 2019) computes the max at stride 1, blurs, then subsamples, and makes CNNs measurably more shift-stable. Shift augmentation helps too.
z_c = frac1H W sum_h, w x[c, h, w]
In words: one number per channel, saying how strongly that channel's feature is present anywhere in the image. The classifier head then reads C numbers instead of H W C :
beginaligned P_flatten &= H W C cdot K + K \\ P_GAP &= C cdot K + K endaligned

Why it replaced flatten: HW times fewer head parameters (VGG's flattened dense head holds most of its 138M parameters), any input size works, the output is invariant to where the object is, and fewer parameters means less overfitting (Network in Network, 2013).

What it loses: where things are. That's fine for classification and wrong when position is the signal. Class activation maps (CAM, Grad-CAM) recover a rough “where” by weighting the last conv maps by each channel's contribution to the class.

Each filter detects one pattern, so output channel o is a map of where pattern o appears. The next layer's filters span all input channels, so they detect combinations of patterns (an edge of this colour next to that texture). Channel counts usually grow with depth while resolution shrinks: there are only a few kinds of edge, but many kinds of object part.
beginaligned y[:, i, j] &= W\, x[:, i, j] + b \\ W &in mathbb R^C_out times C_in endaligned

In words: the same small dense layer applied to every pixel's channel vector, with no mixing across space. It has C_in C_out + C_out parameters and costs H W C_in C_out multiply-adds. It's a per-token linear layer: two 1×1 convs with an activation between them are a transformer's feed-forward block.
Change the channel count cheaply: squeeze channels before an expensive 3×3 (a bottleneck), or project a residual skip so the shapes match.

Mix channels: recombine features that came from elsewhere, such as the branches Inception concatenates, DenseNet's growing stack, U-Net's concatenated skips, or the channels a depthwise conv kept separate.
Add depth cheaply: the 1×1 itself is linear, but the activation after it adds a non-linearity at almost no cost (Network in Network).
Score every pixel: a final 1×1 conv to K channels turns a feature map into per-pixel class scores (FCN, U-Net).
The bottleneck block (ResNet-50 and deeper) squeezes to C/4 channels, runs the 3×3 there, and expands back:
beginaligned P_basic &= 2 cdot 9 C^2 = 18\, C^2 \\ P_bottleneck &= C cdot tfracC4 + 9 big(tfracC4big)^2 + tfracC4 cdot C \\ &= tfrac1716\, C^2 endaligned

In words: two full 3×3 convs on C channels cost 18C^2 ; the bottleneck on the same C channels costs about what a basic block on C/4 channels does ( 18 C^2/16 ). So deep ResNets carry four times wider features at the same cost. The catch: the 3×3 only sees a C/4 -channel summary, an information bottleneck that works because channels are highly redundant (correlated).
A standard conv filters space and mixes channels in one step. MobileNet splits it in two:
Depthwise: one k times k filter per input channel, applied to that channel only.
Pointwise: a 1×1 conv that mixes the channels.
beginaligned cost_std &= H'W' cdot k^2 C_in C_out \\ cost_sep &= H'W' cdot big(k^2 C_in + C_in C_outbig) \\ fraccost_sepcost_std &= frac1C_out + frac1k^2 endaligned

In words: the depthwise step pays k^2 per channel and the pointwise step pays C_in C_out ; dividing by the standard cost leaves two small fractions. With many output channels the first vanishes, so a 3×3 separable conv costs about 1/9 of a standard one, in both multiply-adds and parameters.

The assumption: where to look (spatial filtering) and which channels to combine can be learned separately (Xception's hypothesis). Each layer loses a little accuracy; spending the savings on more channels or layers wins it back.

FLOPs aren't speed: a depthwise conv does only about k^2 multiply-adds per value it reads, with no reuse across channels, so it's limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. MobileNets are fast on phone CPUs but gain far less on a GPU than their FLOP count suggests, because tensor cores need large matrix multiplies to be busy.

MobileNetV2's inverted residual: 1×1 expand (about 6×), 3×3 depthwise, 1×1 project back, with a residual between the narrow ends. The narrow output has no ReLU (a “linear bottleneck”), because a ReLU in a low-dimensional space zeroes whole directions and destroys information.
params = g cdot k^2 cdot fracC_ing cdot fracC_outg = frack^2 C_in C_outg

In words: split the channels into g groups, each with its own conv, and the cost falls g -fold. g = 1 is a standard conv; g = C_in is depthwise. AlexNet used two groups to fit on two GPUs; ResNeXt found that many thin groups (32) beat a wider single path for the same cost. The catch: groups never see each other's channels, so a 1×1 conv or a channel shuffle (ShuffleNet) must follow.
beginaligned mu_c &= frac1N H W sum_n, h, w x_nchw \\ sigma_c^2 &= frac1N H W sum_n, h, w big(x_nchw - mu_cbig)^2 \\ y_nchw &= gamma_c\, fracx_nchw - mu_csqrtsigma_c^2 + epsilon + beta_c endaligned

In words: one mean and one variance per channel, pooled over the batch and every position, with a learned scale gamma_c and shift beta_c . Why per channel and not per position: every position is then normalized the same way, so the layer stays shift-equivariant; per-position statistics would treat the same pattern differently in different places. Pooling over N H W values also makes the estimate much less noisy than in an MLP with the same batch. The general mechanics (why it helps, train vs eval) are in Deep learning basics.

The ReLU sees a standardized input. With BN on the pre-activation, the ReLU's threshold always sits inside the data, so roughly half the units fire. Without it, weight updates can drift a channel all negative (dead: no gradient ever again) or all positive (just linear). gamma and beta let the network choose what fraction fires.
The conv's bias is redundant: BN subtracts the mean, which removes any constant, and beta adds one back. So convs before BN use bias=False.
It's free at inference. With fixed running statistics, BN is a per-channel scale and shift, which folds into the conv just before it:
beginaligned w'_o &= fracgamma_osqrtsigma_o^2 + epsilon\; w_o \\ b'_o &= beta_o + fracgamma_o\, (b_o - mu_o)sqrtsigma_o^2 + epsilon endaligned

In words: scale filter o by its channel's BN gain and fold the shift into the bias; the deployed network has no BN layers at all. A BN placed after the ReLU can only fold into the next conv, and not exactly at the borders, because that conv's zero padding would need to be padding in the normalized space.

BN after the ReLU also trains well (it normalizes the next conv's input instead), and some benchmarks find it equal or marginally better; the difference is small. Pre-activation ResNets use BN → ReLU → conv so that the skip path stays a pure identity.

Without BN: deep plain CNNs train slowly and need a small learning rate and careful He initialization. Deep ResNets can train without it using initialization tricks (Fixup, SkipInit) or NF-Nets with adaptive gradient clipping, but they lose BN's tolerance of high learning rates and its mild regularizing noise.
Depends on the batch; running averages at inference
Batch-independent; ConvNeXt normalizes C at each position
Removes each image's contrast; style transfer
Example and group of channels
Batch-independent; G = 32 is typical

Why GroupNorm: detection and segmentation run at high resolution, so a GPU often holds only one or two images. BN's batch statistics are then very noisy, and the running averages used at test time no longer match what training saw. GroupNorm never looks across the batch, so it behaves the same at any batch size and in training and inference (Wu and He, 2018). It sits between LayerNorm ( G = 1 ) and InstanceNorm ( G = C ), assuming channels within a group share statistics. Alternatives: synchronized BN across GPUs, or frozen BN when fine-tuning (section 10).

ReLU is the CNN default: slope exactly 1 where active, so it doesn't shrink gradients through depth, and it's cheap. Its failure mode in a CNN is the dead filter: a filter whose pre-activation is negative at every position of every image gets zero gradient for good. Leaky ReLU is common in GAN discriminators, SiLU in EfficientNet, GELU in ConvNeXt, and ReLU6 or hard-swish for 8-bit mobile inference. The details are in Activation functions.
Conv, pool, conv, pool, then dense layers; tanh-like units; digits
Showed that weight sharing plus backprop learns features end to end
The same recipe, scaled up on GPUs, with ReLU, dropout and data augmentation
Won ImageNet with a top-5 error of 15.3% against 26.2% for the runner-up, and started the deep-learning era in vision
Only 3×3 convs, stacked 16–19 deep
Same receptive field as large kernels with fewer weights and more non-linearities; a simple, uniform design
Parallel 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 and pooling branches, made affordable by 1×1 reductions; global average pooling
Multi-scale features at a fraction of VGG's parameters
Residual blocks, x + F(x) ; bottlenecks
Fixed the degradation problem, so 100+ layers train
Each layer receives the concatenation of all earlier maps in its block
Feature reuse and short gradient paths with few parameters
Depthwise separable convs; width and resolution multipliers
About k^2 times cheaper layers, for phones
Scale depth, width and resolution together (compound scaling)
Much better accuracy per FLOP than scaling one dimension
A ResNet redesigned with transformer-era choices
A pure CNN matching Swin transformers: much of ViT's edge was recipe and design
VGG: two 3×3s instead of one 5×5
beginaligned P_5 times 5 &= 25\, C^2 \\ P_2 times (3 times 3) &= 18\, C^2 \\ P_7 times 7 &= 49\, C^2 \\ P_3 times (3 times 3) &= 27\, C^2 endaligned
In words: two stacked 3×3 layers see the same 5×5 patch as one 5×5 layer, and three see 7×7, for 18/25 and 27/49 of the weights and multiply-adds, with one or two extra ReLUs in between.

The cost: more layers of activations to store, more sequential steps, and a narrower family of functions. The stack has 18C^2 numbers and a general 5×5 layer 25C^2 , so most 5×5 layers are out of its reach; with a single channel, two 3×3s compose into only a special, factorable 5×5. In practice the extra ReLU makes the stack the better trade. VGG's other lesson was a warning: its flattened dense head holds most of its 138M parameters.
Inception: many kernel sizes at once

Objects appear at different scales, so each block runs 1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 convs and a max pool in parallel and concatenates them. A 1×1 reduction before each large conv shrinks the channels first, or the 5×5 branch would be ruinous. GoogLeNet ended in global average pooling and had about 7M parameters against VGG's 138M; later versions factorized convs further (3×3 into 1×3 then 3×1) and added BatchNorm.

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: The problem: stacking more plain layers past about 20 made training error worse (a 56-layer plain net did worse than a 20-layer one on CIFAR-10). That isn't overfitting. A deeper net could copy the shallower one and set its extra layers to the identity, so its training error should be no worse; the optimizer just couldn't find that solution. Learning an exact identity through a stack of convs and ReLUs is hard.

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: beginaligned x_l+1 &= x_l + F(x_l; W_l) \\ fracpartial Lpartial x_l &= fracpartial Lpartial x_L prod_m=l^L-1 Big(I + fracpartial F_mpartial x_mBig) endaligned

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: In words: each block adds a learned correction to its input. Doing nothing is now the easy default ( F = 0 , which weight decay already pushes towards). Multiplying out the product gives a sum over paths, one of which is the plain identity, so the gradient reaches early layers without being forced through every block's Jacobian ( partial F/partial x , the block's matrix of slopes). When a block changes the width or halves the resolution, the skip becomes a 1×1 conv (stride 2 when the resolution halves), a projection.

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: Two more views: deleting one block from a trained ResNet barely hurts, unlike deleting a layer from VGG, because it behaves like an ensemble of many relatively short paths (Veit et al., 2016); and skips make the loss surface far smoother (Li et al., 2018). More in Deep learning basics.

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: DenseNet: concatenate instead of add

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: beginaligned x_l &= H_lbig([x_0, x_1, dots, x_l-1]big) \\ C_in, l &= C_0 + c_g\,(l - 1) endaligned

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: In words: layer l reads the concatenation of every earlier map in its block and adds c_g new channels (the growth rate, such as 32). Features are reused instead of relearned, and every layer has a short path to the loss; transition layers (1×1 conv, 2×2 average pool) sit between blocks. The cost: every map stays alive for the concatenations, so memory is high, and the growing input width makes later layers slow despite few parameters.

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: MobileNet and EfficientNet: cost-aware design

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: MobileNet builds everything from depthwise separable convs (section 05) and exposes two knobs: a width multiplier alpha on every layer's channels and a resolution multiplier rho on the input, with cost roughly proportional to alpha^2 rho^2 . EfficientNet asks how to spend more compute, and scales all three dimensions together with one coefficient phi :

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: beginaligned depth &= alpha^phi \\ width &= beta^phi \\ resolution &= gamma^phi \\ alpha\, beta^2 gamma^2 &approx 2 endaligned

chunks.h: ResNet: the degradation problem and residuals
chunks.x: In words: FLOPs grow linearly with depth, with the square of width ( C_in and C_out both grow) and with the square of resolution ( H and W both grow), so each step of phi about doubles the FLOPs. alpha, beta, gamma (unrelated to BatchNorm's gamma, beta or MobileNet's alpha ) come from a small grid search on the base network B0, itself found by architecture search. Why together: a higher resolution only helps if the network is deep enough for its receptive field to cover the larger image and wide enough to capture the finer detail; scaling one dimension alone saturates quickly.
